questions.explanation: 细节题。第一段提到本去城里度假一周，请丽莎照顾星星。A、C、D均未在文中提及。

questions.question: Why is Star not happy on the third morning?
choices: A. Lisa gives her a carrot.
B. Lisa comes late.
C. Lisa forgets to clean the stable.
D. Lisa forgets the apple.
questions.explanation: 细节题。第三段说丽莎给了苹果、水和干草，但忘了打扫马厩，所以星星不高兴。A发生在第五天，B发生在第四天，D错误，因为丽莎给了苹果。

questions.question: What does Lisa learn from this story?
choices: A. Horses only eat apples.
B. Holidays are fun.
C. A happy horse needs more than an apple.
D. Friends should not go away.
questions.explanation: 推断题。丽莎在第六段说“我学到了一些东西：一匹快乐的马需要的不仅仅是一个苹果。”这说明她明白了照顾动物需要全面细心。A、B、D都不符合文意。

title: H — The Hat That Helped
text:
Henry had always been a quiet boy. He lived in a small house near the sea with his grandmother. Every day after school, he would walk along the beach, collecting shells and watching the waves. He had few friends, and he often felt invisible.

One cold autumn afternoon, while walking on the beach, Henry found a hat. It was not an ordinary hat. It was made of soft, silver fabric and had a small star stitched on the side. When Henry put it on, something strange happened. He could hear people's thoughts. At first, he was confused. Then he realized that the hat allowed him to understand what others were really thinking.

Henry decided to use the hat to help others. The next day at school, he heard a girl named Lily thinking, "I wish someone would sit with me at lunch." So Henry sat with her. She smiled, and they became friends. Later, he heard a boy thinking, "I'm worried about the math test." Henry offered to study with him. The boy was grateful. Day by day, Henry helped more and more classmates. He no longer felt invisible; he felt needed.

However, one day the hat fell into the sea while Henry was helping a friend. He was sad to lose it. But then he noticed something: he didn't need the hat anymore. He had learned to listen, to notice, and to care. The hat had taught him that everyone has hidden worries and hopes, and that a small act of kindness can make a big difference.

Henry never saw the hat again, but he never forgot its lesson. He grew up to be a kind and thoughtful man, always ready to help those around him. And sometimes, when he walked on the beach, he would smile and remember the silver hat that had changed his life.
translation:
亨利一直是个安静的男孩。他和祖母住在海边的一所小房子里。每天放学后，他都会沿着海滩散步，收集贝壳，看海浪。他朋友很少，常常觉得自己被忽视。

一个寒冷的秋日下午，亨利在海滩上散步时，发现了一顶帽子。这不是一顶普通的帽子。它由柔软、银色的布料制成，侧面缝着一颗小星星。当亨利戴上它时，奇怪的事情发生了。他能听到人们的想法。起初，他很困惑。然后他意识到，这顶帽子让他能够理解别人真正的想法。

亨利决定用这顶帽子去帮助别人。第二天在学校，他听到一个叫莉莉的女孩在想：“我希望有人能和我一起吃午饭。”于是亨利坐到了她旁边。她笑了，他们成了朋友。后来，他听到一个男孩在想：“我担心数学考试。”亨利主动提出和他一起学习。男孩很感激。日复一日，亨利帮助了越来越多的同学。他不再觉得自己被忽视；他感到自己被需要。

然而，有一天，亨利在帮助朋友时，帽子掉进了海里。失去它他很难过。但随后他注意到一件事：他不再需要那顶帽子了。他已经学会了倾听、留意和关心。这顶帽子教会了他，每个人都有隐藏的担忧和希望，一个小小的善举可以带来很大的不同。

亨利再也没有见过那顶帽子，但他从未忘记它的教训。他长大后成了一个善良、体贴的人，总是乐于帮助身边的人。有时，当他在海滩上散步时，他会微笑，想起那顶改变了他生活的银色帽子。

vocabulary.meaning: 看不见的；被忽视的（文中指亨利觉得自己不被注意）
缝制的（文中指星星被缝在帽子上）
教训；道理（文中指帽子带来的启示）

questions.question: What did Henry find on the beach?
choices: A. A silver hat
B. A golden shell
C. A small star
D. A math book
questions.explanation: 细节题。文章第二段提到亨利在海滩上发现了一顶帽子，由银色布料制成。因此选A。

questions.question: Why did Henry no longer feel invisible after using the hat?
choices: A. Because he became rich
B. Because he helped others and felt needed
C. Because he moved to a new house
D. Because he bought a new hat

questions.question: What is the main lesson of the story?
choices: A. Hats can change your life
B. You should always listen to others' thoughts
C. Small acts of kindness can make a big difference
D. It is important to collect shells
questions.explanation: 主旨题。文章最后一段点明主题：每个人都有隐藏的担忧和希望，小小的善举可以带来很大的不同。因此选C。

title: H — The House That Held Its Breath
text:
When Helen inherited her grandmother's house, she expected dust, memories, and perhaps a little regret. What she did not expect was a house that seemed to hold its breath.

The place stood at the end of a lane in a village so quiet that the hedgerows seemed to listen. The front door opened with a sigh, and inside, every piece of furniture was draped in white sheets, like a gathering of polite ghosts. Helen pulled one sheet away and found a piano, its keys yellowed but intact. She pressed middle C. The note rang out, then faded, and the house seemed to exhale.

For the first week, Helen simply lived. She cleaned, sorted, and threw away. But each morning, something small had changed. A chair that she had left by the window now faced the fireplace. A book she had placed on the shelf lay open on the table. Nothing dramatic, nothing threatening, just enough to make her wonder.

She mentioned it to the only neighbour she had met, an elderly man named Arthur who kept bees. Arthur listened, scratched his chin, and said, "Your grandmother used to say the house had opinions. She never argued with it. She just let it have its way."

"That sounds absurd," Helen said.

"Perhaps," Arthur replied. "But you're the one talking to a beekeeper about a house that moves chairs."

Helen laughed, but the laughter didn't quite settle. That night, she sat in the kitchen with a cup of tea, listening to the rain. She thought about her grandmother, a woman who had lived alone for thirty years after her husband died, and who had never once complained of loneliness. Helen had always assumed this was strength. Now she wondered if the house had been company, or if her grandmother had simply learned to be still.

The following afternoon, Helen found a small notebook in the piano bench. The handwriting was her grandmother's, neat and unhurried. It was not a diary but a list of small observations: the first frost, a neighbour's new baby, the moment the lilacs bloomed. On the last page, one sentence stood alone: "A house remembers what we forget to say."

Helen closed the notebook. She looked at the piano, the sheets, the chair that had moved. She understood, finally, that none of it was magic. Her grandmother had spent decades arranging and rearranging her small world, talking to the walls, listening for the house's opinion. The house did not move on its own. It moved because someone had once cared enough to make it alive.

That evening, Helen did not cover the piano. She left the notebook on the table, the chair by the window, the sheets folded in a neat pile. She played a simple tune, badly, and the house seemed to lean in. For the first time since the funeral, she did not feel like a visitor.

Arthur came by the next day with a jar of honey. He looked at the piano, then at Helen.

"The house seems different," he said.

"It's just a house," Helen said.

Arthur smiled. "So is a beehive. But you'd be surprised what a little attention does."

Helen stayed. She did not sell. And slowly, over months, the house stopped holding its breath, because there was finally someone to breathe with.
translation:
当海伦继承她祖母的房子时，她预料到会有灰尘、回忆，或许还有一点点遗憾。她没有预料到的，是一栋仿佛屏住呼吸的房子。

房子坐落在一条小巷尽头，村庄安静得连树篱都像在倾听。前门开时发出一声叹息，里面每件家具都罩着白布，像一群彬彬有礼的鬼魂在聚会。海伦拉开一块布，发现一架钢琴，琴键泛黄但完好。她按下中央C。音符响起，然后渐渐消失，房子似乎呼出一口气。

第一周，海伦只是住着。她打扫、整理、丢弃。但每天早晨，总有微小的变化。她留在窗边的椅子现在面向壁炉。她放在书架上的书摊开在桌上。没什么大事，也没什么威胁，只是足以让她起疑。

她跟唯一认识的邻居提起这件事，一个养蜂的老人，名叫亚瑟。亚瑟听着，挠挠下巴说：“你祖母以前说这房子有自己的想法。她从不跟它争。她只是让它按自己的意思来。”

“那听起来很荒谬，”海伦说。

“也许吧，”亚瑟回答。“但你现在正是在跟一个养蜂人谈论一栋会移动椅子的房子。”

海伦笑了，但笑声没有完全落下。那天晚上，她坐在厨房里，端着一杯茶，听雨。她想起祖母，一个丈夫去世后独居三十年的女人，从未抱怨过孤独。海伦一直以为那是坚强。现在她想，也许房子曾是陪伴，或者祖母只是学会了安静。

第二天下午，海伦在钢琴凳里发现一个小笔记本。笔迹是祖母的，工整而从容。不是日记，而是一份细小观察的清单：初霜、邻居的新生儿、丁香开花的那一刻。最后一页，单独写着一句话：“房子记得我们忘记说的话。”

海伦合上笔记本。她看着钢琴、白布、移动过的椅子。她终于明白，这一切都不是魔法。祖母几十年来一直在安排和重新安排她的小世界，对着墙壁说话，倾听房子的意见。房子并不会自己移动。它移动，是因为曾经有人在乎到让它活起来。

那天晚上，海伦没有盖上钢琴。她把笔记本留在桌上，椅子留在窗边，白布折成整齐的一摞。她弹了一首简单的曲子，弹得很糟，而房子似乎凑了过来。自葬礼以来第一次，她不再觉得自己是个访客。

亚瑟第二天带着一罐蜂蜜来访。他看看钢琴，又看看海伦。

“房子好像不一样了，”他说。

“它只是一栋房子，”海伦说。

亚瑟笑了。“蜂巢也是。但你会惊讶，一点关注能带来什么。”

海伦留下了。她没有卖房。慢慢地，几个月过去，房子不再屏住呼吸，因为终于有人和它一起呼吸了。

vocabulary.meaning: 树篱（乡间路边或田边的一排灌木）
用布覆盖、悬挂（文中指用白布罩住家具）
从容不迫的，不慌不忙的
凑近；倾身靠近（文中指房子仿佛在倾听）

questions.question: What is the main reason the house seems to change?
choices: A. It is haunted by a ghost.
B. Helen's grandmother arranged things and cared for it, making it feel alive.
C. Arthur secretly moves the furniture.
D. The house has magical powers.
questions.explanation: 文章结尾说明，房子并不会自己移动，而是因为祖母曾经用心安排、照料，使它充满生机。因此B正确。A、D是海伦最初的猜测，C文中没有依据。

questions.question: Why does Helen decide to stay in the house?
choices: A. She cannot afford to move.
B. Arthur asks her to stay.
C. She realizes the house can be company if she gives it attention.
D. She wants to sell it for a higher price.
questions.explanation: 海伦通过笔记本和亚瑟的话，意识到房子之所以有“生命”，是因为有人关注。她选择留下并弹琴，说明她愿意成为那个给予关注的人。C最符合文意。

questions.question: What does Arthur's comment about the beehive suggest?
choices: A. Bees are more important than houses.
B. A little attention can bring a place or relationship to life.
C. Helen should become a beekeeper.
D. Houses and beehives are exactly the same.
questions.explanation: 亚瑟说“蜂巢也是。但你会惊讶，一点关注能带来什么。”他在暗示，就像蜂巢需要照料一样，房子也需要人的关注才能有生气。B最准确。

title: I — The Ice Cream Island
text:
Tom lives in a small town by the sea. Every summer, he goes to the beach with his dog, Lucky. They love to play in the water and run on the sand.

One hot day, Tom sees a small boat near the beach. An old man sits in the boat. He has a big box of ice cream. "Hello, boy!" the man says. "Do you want some ice cream?" Tom says yes. The old man gives him a big ice cream. It is cold and sweet.

"Where do you come from?" Tom asks. "I come from Ice Cream Island," the man says. "It is a small island far away. On that island, we make ice cream all day. We have many flavors: mango, banana, and even carrot!" Tom thinks it is a fun place. He wants to visit it.

The old man says, "You can come with me. But first, you must help me sell all this ice cream." Tom says yes. He runs home and tells his mother. She says, "OK, but come back before dinner."

Tom and the old man go to the town. They walk from street to street. Many children buy ice cream. Tom is good at selling. He smiles and says, "Try this mango ice cream! It is very good!" Soon, the box is empty.

"You are a good helper," the old man says. "Now we can go to the island." But Tom looks at the sea. The sky is dark. A big wind comes. "We cannot go now," the old man says. "The sea is not safe. Maybe next summer."

Tom is a little sad. But he thinks about the island. Next summer, he will see it. He will eat ice cream all day. He smiles and runs home with Lucky.

That night, Tom dreams of Ice Cream Island. In his dream, the island is made of ice cream. He swims in a sea of milk and eats sweet clouds. It is the best dream ever.
translation:
汤姆住在海边的一个小镇上。每年夏天，他都会带着他的狗“幸运”去海滩。他们喜欢在水里玩，在沙滩上跑。

一个炎热的日子，汤姆在海滩附近看到一只小船。一位老人坐在船里。他有一大盒冰淇淋。“你好，孩子！”老人说。“你想要一些冰淇淋吗？”汤姆说好。老人给了他一个大冰淇淋。它又冷又甜。

“你从哪里来？”汤姆问。“我从冰淇淋岛来，”老人说。“那是一个很远的小岛。在那个岛上，我们整天做冰淇淋。我们有很多口味：芒果、香蕉，甚至胡萝卜！”汤姆觉得那是个有趣的地方。他想去那里看看。

老人说：“你可以跟我来。但首先，你必须帮我把所有这些冰淇淋卖掉。”汤姆答应了。他跑回家告诉了妈妈。她说：“好吧，但要在晚饭前回来。”

汤姆和老人去了镇上。他们走过一条又一条街。许多孩子买了冰淇淋。汤姆很会卖。他微笑着说：“试试这个芒果冰淇淋！它非常好吃！”很快，盒子空了。

“你是个好帮手，”老人说。“现在我们可以去岛上了。”但汤姆看着大海。天空很暗。一阵大风吹来。“我们现在不能去，”老人说。“海上不安全。也许明年夏天吧。”

汤姆有点伤心。但他想着那个岛。明年夏天，他会看到它。他会整天吃冰淇淋。他微笑着，和“幸运”一起跑回家。

那天晚上，汤姆梦见了冰淇淋岛。在他的梦里，那个岛是冰淇淋做的。他在牛奶的海洋里游泳，吃着甜甜的云朵。这是有史以来最好的梦。

questions.question: What does the old man give Tom?
choices: A. A boat
B. A box
C. An ice cream
D. A dog
questions.explanation: 细节题。根据第二段，老人给了汤姆一个大冰淇淋，因此选C。

questions.question: Why can't Tom and the old man go to the island?
choices: A. Tom is tired.
B. The sea is not safe.
C. The boat is too small.
D. They have no ice cream.
questions.explanation: 细节题。根据第五段，老人说“The sea is not safe.”，所以不能去岛上，选B。

questions.question: What can we learn from the story?
choices: A. Tom doesn't like ice cream.
B. The old man lives in Tom's town.
C. Tom will visit the island next summer.
D. Lucky sells ice cream with Tom.
questions.explanation: 推断题。根据倒数第二段“Next summer, he will see it.”，可以推断汤姆明年夏天会去岛上，选C。

title: I — The Island of Lost Sounds
text:
It was a small island, no bigger than a football field, and it appeared on no map. Leo had been sailing alone for three days when a storm broke his mast. He drifted for hours until the current pushed his little boat onto a beach of white sand. The island was covered with tall grass and strange blue flowers. There was no sign of human life, but Leo heard something odd: a soft, humming sound, like hundreds of voices whispering at once.

He walked toward the sound and found a circle of black stones. Inside the circle, the air felt heavy. Leo stepped closer. Suddenly, he heard his mother's voice calling his name. Then his best friend laughing. Then his own voice, from years ago, saying, "I'm sorry." The sounds seemed to come from the stones. Leo touched one, and the humming stopped for a moment. He pulled his hand back. The sounds returned.

On the second day, Leo explored the island more carefully. He found a small cave behind a waterfall. Inside, there were walls covered with drawings — people holding hands, children playing, a dog running. Under the drawings, someone had written a sentence in English: "We leave our voices here so we can listen to the world." Leo sat down, confused. He had never heard of such a place. But as he sat there, he realized something: he had been talking for years, but he had rarely listened. He had missed the soft sounds of his mother's tired sigh, his friend's silent worry. He had been too busy with his own voice.

On the third day, a fishing boat appeared. The fishermen were surprised to see Leo. "How did you get here?" they asked. "This island is called the Island of Lost Sounds. Sailors say it only appears to people who need to hear something important." Leo smiled. He understood now.

When he returned home, he did not tell anyone about the island. But he began to listen — really listen — to the people around him. And sometimes, when the wind blew softly, he thought he could still hear the humming of the stones, reminding him that the world has a voice, if only we stop to hear it.
translation:
那是一座小岛，不比一个足球场大，而且不在地图上。利奥独自航行了三天，这时一场风暴折断了桅杆。他漂流了几个小时，直到水流把他的一叶小舟推上一片白沙滩。岛上覆盖着高高的草和奇异的蓝色花朵。没有人类的迹象，但利奥听到了奇怪的东西：一种轻柔的嗡嗡声，像成百上千个声音同时低语。

他朝声音走去，发现一圈黑色的石头。圆圈内，空气感觉沉重。利奥走近了些。突然，他听到母亲在叫他的名字。接着是他最好的朋友在笑。然后是他自己多年前的声音，说着：“对不起。”声音似乎来自那些石头。利奥摸了一块石头，嗡嗡声停了一瞬。他把手抽回来，声音又回来了。

第二天，利奥更仔细地探索了这座岛。他在瀑布后面发现了一个小洞穴。洞内的墙壁上画满了画——人们手拉手、孩子们玩耍、一只狗在跑。在画的下面，有人用英语写了一个句子：“我们把声音留在这里，以便聆听世界。”利奥困惑地坐下。他从未听说过这样的地方。但当他坐在那里时，他意识到了一些事情：他多年来一直在说话，却很少倾听。他错过了母亲疲惫的叹息、朋友无声的忧虑这些细微的声音。他太忙于自己的声音了。

第三天，一艘渔船出现了。渔民们看到利奥很惊讶。“你怎么到这里的？”他们问。“这座岛叫失落声音之岛。水手们说它只出现在需要听到重要事情的人面前。”利奥笑了。他现在明白了。

回到家后，他没有告诉任何人关于这座岛的事。但他开始倾听——真正地倾听——他周围的人。有时，当风轻轻吹过，他觉得自己仍能听到石头的嗡嗡声，提醒他世界有声音，只要我们停下来去听。

vocabulary.meaning: 漂流；文中指船在海上随水流漂浮
嗡嗡声；文中指石头发出的一种低沉的连续声音
低语，耳语；文中指声音像轻声说话
探索；文中指利奥仔细查看岛屿
困惑的；文中指利奥对所见所闻感到不解
很少；文中指利奥几乎不倾听
叹息；文中指母亲疲惫的叹气声
提醒；文中指嗡嗡声让利奥想起要倾听
出现；文中指岛屿只对需要的人显现
倾听；文中指真正用心去听别人说话

questions.question: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: A. A boy gets lost at sea and is rescued by fishermen.
B. A boy discovers an island where he learns the importance of listening.
C. A boy finds a cave with ancient drawings and becomes famous.
D. A boy builds a new boat after a storm destroys his old one.
questions.explanation: 主旨题。文章讲述利奥漂流到一座神秘岛屿，在岛上经历后意识到自己过去很少倾听，回家后开始真正倾听他人。B项准确概括了故事核心。A项只涉及开头和结尾的救援，不是主旨；C项中“成名”文中未提；D项与故事重点无关。

questions.question: What did Leo realize while sitting in the cave?
choices: A. He had been talking too much and listening too little.
B. He had forgotten his mother's phone number.
C. He had seen the island on a map before.
D. He had lost his voice completely.
questions.explanation: 细节题。文中明确写道：“he had been talking for years, but he had rarely listened”，即他多年来一直在说话，却很少倾听。A项正确。B、C、D项文中均未提及。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the island from the fishermen's words?
choices: A. The island is easy to find for anyone who looks for it.
B. The island disappears when people try to speak.
C. The island only appears to people who need to hear something important.
D. The island is a popular tourist destination.
questions.explanation: 推断题。渔民说：“This island is called the Island of Lost Sounds. Sailors say it only appears to people who need to hear something important.” 由此可推断，岛屿只对需要听到重要事情的人显现。C项正确。A、D项与文意相反；B项文中未提。

title: I — The Invention of the Umbrella
text:
In the quaint town of Bellwood, where rain was as frequent as gossip, there lived an inventor named Elias Thorne. His workshop, cluttered with gears and half-finished contraptions, was a testament to his restless mind. Yet, despite his ingenuity, Elias had never created anything that truly mattered to the townsfolk—until the day he noticed something peculiar.

It was a drizzly afternoon when Elias stood by his window, watching people scurry through the downpour. They clutched newspapers over their heads, only to have them dissolve into pulp within minutes. Children wailed as their mothers dragged them through puddles, and old Mr. Higgins, the baker, slipped on the wet cobblestones, scattering his precious loaves into the mud. Elias frowned. 'There must be a better way,' he murmured.

That evening, as he sat by the fire, an idea began to germinate. He recalled a trip to the Orient years ago, where he had seen paper parasols used against the sun. What if he could fashion something similar, but waterproof? He spent the next fortnight experimenting with oiled silk, whalebone ribs, and a collapsible mechanism. His fingers bled from countless pricks, and his savings dwindled as he purchased materials, but he persisted.

Finally, on a gray morning, he emerged from his workshop holding a curious object: a canopy of oiled silk stretched over a frame of bamboo, with a handle that allowed it to be folded. He called it the 'umbrella,' from the Latin word for shade. But when he walked through the market square, people stared and whispered. 'What is that absurd thing?' scoffed Mrs. Pemberton, the mayor's wife. 'Only a fool would carry a tent on a stick.' Elias's heart sank, but he forced a smile.

Days turned into weeks, and the umbrella remained a curiosity. Then came the Great Storm. The skies turned black, and rain fell in sheets. The river burst its banks, flooding the streets. People huddled in their homes, terrified. Elias, undeterred, grabbed his umbrella and waded into the deluge. He found Mrs. Pemberton trapped in her carriage, water rising around her. Without hesitation, he extended the umbrella and helped her to safety. Others soon followed, using Elias's invention to shield themselves from the relentless rain.

Overnight, Elias became a hero. The townsfolk clamored for umbrellas, and he gladly taught them how to make their own. Mrs. Pemberton, her pride humbled, commissioned a special umbrella lined with lace. And old Mr. Higgins, whose bakery had been saved from flooding, named a new pastry after Elias: the 'Thorne Tart.'

As Elias sat in his workshop, watching the rain patter against the window, he realized that invention was not about grand accolades or wealth. It was about solving the small, everyday problems that plagued people's lives. His umbrella, once mocked, now stood as a symbol of resilience and ingenuity. And as he looked at the sky, he smiled, knowing that even the darkest storm could bring forth a silver lining.

In Bellwood, rain was still frequent, but now it was greeted with a chorus of snapping umbrellas—a sound that echoed the triumph of a persistent inventor who dared to think differently.
translation:
在古雅的贝尔伍德小镇，雨水和流言一样频繁，这里住着一位名叫埃利亚斯·索恩的发明家。他的工作坊里堆满了齿轮和半成品的装置，见证着他永不停歇的头脑。然而，尽管他心灵手巧，埃利亚斯从未创造出任何对镇民真正重要的东西——直到有一天，他注意到了一件奇怪的事。

那是一个细雨绵绵的下午，埃利亚斯站在窗边，看着人们在倾盆大雨中匆匆奔走。他们把报纸顶在头上，结果几分钟内报纸就化成了纸浆。孩子们在母亲拽着他们穿过水坑时号啕大哭，而老希金斯先生，那位面包师，在湿滑的鹅卵石上滑倒，把他珍贵的面包撒了一地泥。埃利亚斯皱起了眉头。“一定有更好的办法，”他喃喃自语。

那天晚上，他坐在火炉边，一个想法开始萌芽。他回忆起多年前的一次东方之旅，在那里他见过用来遮阳的纸伞。如果他能做出类似的东西，但是防水的呢？接下来的两周，他用油绸、鲸骨伞骨和一个可折叠的机械装置进行实验。他的手指被无数次刺破流血，积蓄也因购买材料而减少，但他坚持了下来。

终于，在一个灰蒙蒙的早晨，他走出工作坊，手里拿着一个奇特的物件：一块油绸伞面撑在竹制伞架上，带有一个可以折叠的把手。他称之为“umbrella”，源自拉丁语中“遮荫”一词。但当他走过集市广场时，人们盯着看，窃窃私语。“那是什么荒唐的东西？”市长的妻子彭伯顿夫人嗤笑道。“只有傻子才会在棍子上顶个帐篷。”埃利亚斯的心沉了下去，但他强颜欢笑。

日子一天天过去，雨伞依然是个稀奇玩意儿。然后大风暴来了。天空变得漆黑，大雨倾盆而下。河水决堤，淹没了街道。人们蜷缩在家里，惊恐万分。埃利亚斯没有被吓倒，他抓起雨伞，涉入洪流。他发现彭伯顿夫人被困在马车里，水在她周围上涨。他毫不犹豫地撑开雨伞，帮她转移到安全地带。其他人也纷纷效仿，用埃利亚斯的发明来遮挡无情的雨水。

一夜之间，埃利亚斯成了英雄。镇民们争相索要雨伞，他乐意教他们如何自己制作。彭伯顿夫人放下了骄傲，定制了一把镶有蕾丝边的特殊雨伞。而老希金斯先生，他的面包房因免于水淹，以埃利亚斯的名字命名了一种新糕点：“索恩挞”。

埃利亚斯坐在工作坊里，看着雨点敲打窗户，他意识到发明不是为了显赫的荣誉或财富。而是为了解决困扰人们生活的日常小问题。他的雨伞，曾被嘲笑，如今成为坚韧和创造力的象征。当他望向天空时，他微笑着，知道即使是最黑暗的风暴也能带来一线希望。

在贝尔伍德，雨仍然频繁，但现在迎接它的是此起彼伏的雨伞张开声——这声音回响着一位敢于不同思考的执着发明家的胜利。

questions.question: What was the initial reaction of the townspeople to Elias's umbrella?
choices: A. They were amazed and wanted to buy it immediately.
B. They mocked and ridiculed it.
C. They ignored it completely.
D. They thought it was a new kind of tent.
questions.explanation: 细节题。文章第四段提到，当埃利亚斯带着雨伞走过集市时，人们盯着看并窃窃私语，彭伯顿夫人嘲笑说‘只有傻子才会在棍子上顶个帐篷’，说明最初人们是嘲笑和讥讽的。A、C、D均与原文不符。

questions.question: Why did Elias decide to invent the umbrella?
choices: A. He wanted to become famous and wealthy.
B. He was inspired by a trip to the Orient and saw a need to solve a problem.
C. He was ordered by the mayor to create something useful.
D. He wanted to impress Mrs. Pemberton.
questions.explanation: 推断题。文章第三段提到，埃利亚斯回忆起东方之旅中见过的纸伞，并思考能否做出防水的类似物；第二段描述了他看到人们被雨淋的困境，因此他发明雨伞是为了解决实际问题，同时受到东方之旅的启发。A、C、D均不是主要原因。

questions.question: What does the story suggest about the nature of invention?
choices: A. Inventions must be grand and expensive to be valuable.
B. Inventions often face initial resistance but can solve everyday problems.
C. Inventions are only successful if they make money.
D. Inventions should always be kept secret.
questions.explanation: 主旨题。文章最后一段点明，发明不是为了荣誉或财富，而是解决困扰人们生活的日常小问题；雨伞最初被嘲笑，后来却成为英雄，说明发明常常面临最初的阻力，但能解决实际问题。A、C、D均与文章主旨相悖。

title: Journey to the Jungle
text:
Jack is a young reporter. He works for a small newspaper. One day, his boss says, "Jack, go to the jungle. Find a story about the lost city."

Jack is afraid. He likes cities, not jungles. But he says yes. He takes a bus, then a boat, then walks for many hours. The jungle is hot and green. He hears birds and monkeys. He sees big trees and small rivers. He is tired but he walks on.

At night, Jack sits by a fire. An old man comes to him. The man says, "I know the lost city. Follow me." Jack follows the old man. They walk all night.

In the morning, they stop. Jack looks around. He sees no city. Only trees. "Where is the city?" Jack asks. The old man smiles. "The city is under your feet," he says. "Long ago, people lived here. But the jungle took it back." Jack looks down. He sees old stones in the grass. He takes photos and writes notes.

Jack goes home. His boss reads the story. "This is a good story," the boss says. Jack smiles. He is not afraid of the jungle now. He learns that stories are everywhere. You just need to open your eyes.
translation:
杰克是一名年轻记者。他在一家小报社工作。一天，老板说：“杰克，去丛林。找一个关于失落之城的故事。”

杰克很害怕。他喜欢城市，不喜欢丛林。但他说好。他坐公交车，然后坐船，然后走了很多小时。丛林又热又绿。他听到鸟和猴子的声音。他看到大树和小河。他很累，但他继续走。

晚上，杰克坐在火边。一个老人向他走来。老人说：“我知道失落之城。跟我来。”杰克跟着老人。他们走了一整夜。

早上，他们停下来。杰克环顾四周。他没有看到城市。只有树。“城市在哪里？”杰克问。老人笑了。“城市在你脚下，”他说。“很久以前，人们住在这里。但丛林把它收回了。”杰克低头看。他看到草地里的旧石头。他拍照并做笔记。

杰克回家。老板读了故事。“这是个好故事，”老板说。杰克笑了。他现在不怕丛林了。他学到故事无处不在。你只需要睁开眼睛。

questions.question: What does Jack's boss ask him to do?
choices: A. Go to a city and take photos.
B. Go to the jungle and find a story.
C. Write a story about his family.
D. Stay in the office and write.
questions.explanation: 文章第一段老板说：“杰克，去丛林。找一个关于失落之城的故事。”所以选B。

questions.question: Why does Jack go with the old man?
choices: A. Because the old man is his friend.
B. Because the old man knows the lost city.
C. Because the old man gives him money.
D. Because the old man is his boss.
questions.explanation: 第三段老人说：“我知道失落之城。跟我来。”杰克因此跟着他。所以选B。

questions.question: What does Jack learn from his trip?
choices: A. The jungle is a dangerous place.
B. Old men are always right.
C. Stories are everywhere if you look.
D. Cities are better than jungles.
questions.explanation: 最后一段杰克学到“故事无处不在。你只需要睁开眼睛。”所以选C。

title: Journey to the Jungle's Heart
text:
Jason had always dreamed of becoming a journalist who reported from the world's most remote places. When he was offered a chance to join an expedition into the Amazon rainforest, he packed his bag without hesitation. His task was to write a feature story about a lost plant that might cure a rare disease.

The team, led by Dr. Silva, consisted of five scientists and two local guides. They set off from a small village and soon entered the thick jungle. The air was hot and wet, and strange sounds came from every direction. Jason took photos and notes, feeling both excited and nervous.

As days passed, the journey became tougher. They had to cut through vines, cross muddy rivers, and climb over fallen trees. One afternoon, a sudden storm forced them to stop. While they were waiting, Jason noticed an old notebook in Dr. Silva's bag. He opened it and found pages of careful drawings and notes about the lost plant. "You've already found it?" Jason asked in surprise. Dr. Silva smiled. "Not yet. But I've been close for years. This trip is my last chance."

The next morning, one of the guides fell ill with a high fever. The team had to decide whether to continue or turn back. Dr. Silva looked at the sick man and said, "We can't risk his life. We'll return." Jason felt disappointed, but he understood.

On the way back, Jason accidentally slipped down a small hill and landed near a stream. When he stood up, he saw a bright purple flower growing on a rock. It matched the drawing in Dr. Silva's notebook exactly! He called the team, and they carefully collected samples.

Back in the village, Dr. Silva confirmed that the flower was indeed the lost plant. It contained a powerful substance that could treat the disease. Jason's article about the journey was published in a major newspaper and attracted worldwide attention.

Jason learned that success doesn't always come from pushing forward. Sometimes, turning back can lead to a surprising discovery.
translation:
杰森一直梦想成为一名在世界最偏远地区报道的记者。当他得到一个加入亚马逊雨林探险队的机会时，他毫不犹豫地收拾了行李。他的任务是写一篇关于一种可能治愈罕见疾病的失传植物的专题报道。

由席尔瓦博士带领的团队由五名科学家和两名当地向导组成。他们从一个小村庄出发，很快进入了茂密的丛林。空气又热又湿，奇怪的声音从四面八方传来。杰森拍照并做笔记，既兴奋又紧张。

随着日子一天天过去，旅程变得更加艰难。他们不得不砍断藤蔓，穿过泥泞的河流，爬过倒下的树木。一天下午，一场突如其来的暴风雨迫使他们停下来。在等待的时候，杰森注意到席尔瓦博士包里有一个旧笔记本。他打开它，发现里面写满了关于那种失传植物的仔细绘图和笔记。“你已经找到它了？”杰森惊讶地问。席尔瓦博士笑了。“还没有。但我已经接近它很多年了。这次旅行是我最后的机会。”

第二天早上，一名向导发高烧病倒了。团队必须决定是继续前进还是返回。席尔瓦博士看着病人说：“我们不能拿他的生命冒险。我们回去。”杰森感到失望，但他理解。

在回去的路上，杰森不小心滑下一个小山丘，落在一条小溪附近。当他站起来时，他看到一块岩石上长着一朵亮紫色的花。它与席尔瓦博士笔记本上的图画完全吻合！他叫来了团队，他们小心地采集了样本。

回到村庄后，席尔瓦博士确认这朵花确实是那种失传的植物。它含有一种可以治疗这种疾病的强效物质。杰森关于这次旅程的文章发表在一家大报纸上，引起了全世界的关注。

杰森认识到，成功并不总是来自勇往直前。有时候，回头反而能带来意想不到的发现。

questions.question: What was Jason's main task in the expedition?
choices: A. To find the lost plant by himself.
B. To write a feature story about the lost plant.
C. To guide the team through the jungle.
D. To treat the sick guide.
questions.explanation: 第一段最后一句提到“His task was to write a feature story about a lost plant...”，因此答案是B。A项说他自己找植物，但实际是团队一起；C项他是记者不是向导；D项治疗病人是医生的事。

questions.question: Why did the team decide to turn back?
choices: A. They were lost in the jungle.
B. The weather was too bad.
C. One of the guides became seriously ill.
D. Dr. Silva had found the plant already.
questions.explanation: 第四段提到“one of the guides fell ill with a high fever”并且席尔瓦博士说“We can't risk his life. We'll return.”，所以原因是向导病重，选C。A、B、D均与原文不符。

questions.question: What did Jason learn from the journey?
choices: A. Never give up your dream.
B. jungle is full of dangers.
C. Sometimes turning back can lead to a surprising discovery.
D. Journalists should always take photos.
questions.explanation: 最后一段明确点出“Jason learned that success doesn't always come from pushing forward. Sometimes, turning back can lead to a surprising discovery.”，因此选C。A、B、D虽然部分合理，但不是文章强调的道理。

title: J — The Jam Jar Journal
text:
Journalist Helen Marsh was known for her biting investigative pieces, but the assignment that landed on her desk was far from her usual beat. Her editor wanted a soft feature on a struggling artisan jam maker in the countryside. Helen groaned inwardly; she preferred exposing corruption to writing about fruit preserves. Nevertheless, she drove to the address, a dilapidated farmhouse where a wiry old man named Arthur greeted her with a wary nod.

Arthur led her into a chaotic kitchen, where copper pots hung like trophies and the air was thick with the scent of simmering berries. He spoke little, but his hands moved with a precision that betrayed decades of practice. Helen, initially dismissive, found herself captivated by his quiet dedication. She asked routine questions, scribbling notes, but gradually her curiosity deepened. Why did he continue when supermarkets sold jam for a fraction of his price? "Because," Arthur said, "each jar is a conversation. You can't rush a conversation."

As days turned into weeks, Helen returned repeatedly, supposedly for research. She helped stir a batch of damson jam, her hands stained purple, and listened to Arthur's stories: how he had inherited the orchard, how a blight had nearly ruined him, how he had rebuilt from a single surviving tree. She realized his struggle mirrored her own: both were clinging to something authentic in a world that favored the cheap and the fast. Her editor called, pressing for the piece, but Helen hesitated. The story felt too intimate to reduce to column inches.

One morning, Arthur handed her a jar from a hidden shelf. The label was handwritten: "For the journalist who listens." Inside, the jam was dark and complex, with a hint of rosemary. "You're not here just for a story," he said. "You're looking for a reason to care again." Helen was stunned; he had seen through her professional armor. She had been going through the motions, churning out articles without heart, ever since a major investigation had collapsed under legal threats.

That night, she wrote not an exposé but a narrative—a portrait of a man and his orchard, and of herself, a seeker of truth in unexpected places. The article, titled "The Jam Jar Journal," was published to wide acclaim. Readers wrote to say it reminded them of what mattered. Helen didn't win a Pulitzer, but she rediscovered her purpose. She kept the empty jar on her desk, a reminder that the most profound stories are often the quietest, and that listening is sometimes the bravest act of all.
translation:
记者海伦·马什以尖锐的调查报道闻名，但落到她桌上的任务却远非她所长。编辑想要一篇关于乡下一位苦苦挣扎的手工果酱制作人的软文。海伦内心呻吟；她更喜欢揭露腐败，而不是写水果蜜饯。尽管如此，她还是驱车前往那个地址——一座破败的农舍，一位精瘦的老人亚瑟警惕地点头招呼她。

亚瑟带她走进混乱的厨房，铜锅像战利品一样悬挂着，空气中弥漫着炖煮浆果的浓郁气味。他话不多，但他的双手动作精准，透露出数十年的练习。海伦最初不以为然，却发现自己被他的默默专注所吸引。她问着常规问题，草草记着笔记，但好奇心逐渐加深。为什么在超市以他价格零头出售果酱时，他还要继续？"因为，"亚瑟说，"每一罐都是一次对话。你不能催促对话。"

日子变成数周，海伦反复回来，据说是为了研究。她帮忙搅拌一批西洋李果酱，双手染成紫色，听着亚瑟的故事：他如何继承果园，一场枯萎病几乎毁了他，他如何从一棵幸存的树重建。她意识到他的挣扎映照了她自己的：两人都在一个偏爱廉价和快速的世界里，坚守着某种真实。她的编辑打电话催稿，但海伦犹豫了。这个故事太私密，无法压缩成专栏尺寸。

一天早晨，亚瑟从隐藏的架子上递给她一罐。标签是手写的："给倾听的记者。"里面的果酱深色而复杂，带有一丝迷迭香。"你来这里不只为了一篇报道，"他说。"你在寻找再次关心的理由。"海伦惊呆了；他看穿了她的职业盔甲。自一项重大调查在法律威胁下崩溃以来，她一直在机械地应付，炮制没有心的文章。

那晚，她写的不是揭露，而是一篇叙述——一个男人和他的果园的画像，以及她自己，一个在意想不到的地方寻找真相的人。这篇题为《果酱罐日记》的文章出版后广受赞誉。读者写信说它提醒了他们什么才是重要的。海伦没有赢得普利策奖，但她重新发现了自己的目标。她把空罐子留在桌上，提醒自己：最深刻的故事往往最安静，而倾听有时是最勇敢的行为。

questions.question: What is the main theme of the story?
choices: A. The importance of traditional jam-making techniques.
B. A journalist's journey to rediscover her passion through an unexpected encounter.
C. The rivalry between artisanal and commercial food producers.
D. The challenges of investigative journalism in the countryside.
questions.explanation: 文章主旨是海伦通过采访果酱制作人亚瑟，重新发现了自己对写作的热情和目的。A、C、D均为细节或次要内容。

questions.question: Why did Helen hesitate to write the article at first?
choices: A. She thought the story was too intimate to reduce to a simple piece.
B. She was too busy with another investigation.
C. She didn't like Arthur's jam.
D. She was afraid of legal threats.
questions.explanation: 文中提到' The story felt too intimate to reduce to column inches.'，即她认为故事太私密，无法压缩成专栏。B、C、D均无依据。

questions.question: What can be inferred about Arthur from the story?
choices: A. He was a former journalist.
B. He inherited the orchard and faced a blight.
C. He was eager for publicity.
D. He disliked Helen from the start.
questions.explanation: 文中明确提到亚瑟继承了果园并遭遇枯萎病（inherited the orchard, a blight had nearly ruined him），因此B正确。A、C、D均与原文不符。

title: K — The Kind Kangaroo
text:
Kangaroo Kim lives in a big park in Australia. She has a small baby in her pocket. Every morning, she jumps and looks for food. She is very kind.

One day, Kim sees a little bird. The bird cannot fly. Its wing is hurt. "Help me, please," says the bird. "I cannot go home."

Kim looks at the bird. She wants to help. But the bird's home is in a tall tree. Kim cannot climb trees. She is too big and heavy.

Kim thinks for a minute. Then she has an idea. She asks her friend, Koala Ken, for help. Ken lives in the tall tree. He can climb very well.

"Ken, can you help this little bird?" asks Kim. "It cannot fly home. Its wing is hurt."

Ken looks at the bird. "Of course," he says. "I can take it home. But I need a soft place for it."

Kim smiles. She takes some soft grass from the ground. She makes a little bed with the grass. Then Ken takes the bird and climbs up the tree. He puts the bird in its nest.

The bird is very happy. "Thank you, Kim! Thank you, Ken!" it says. "You are kind friends."

Kim jumps back to her baby. She feels good. She knows that when we help others, we feel happy too.
translation:
袋鼠金住在澳大利亚的一个大公园里。她的口袋里有一个小宝宝。每天早上，她跳来跳去地寻找食物。她非常善良。

有一天，金看到一只小鸟。这只鸟不能飞。它的翅膀受伤了。“请帮帮我，”小鸟说。“我回不了家了。”

金看着小鸟。她想帮忙。但是小鸟的家在一棵高高的树上。金不会爬树。她太大太重了。

金想了一会儿。然后她有了一个主意。她向她的朋友考拉肯求助。肯住在那棵高高的树上。他非常会爬树。

“肯，你能帮帮这只小鸟吗？”金问。“它不能飞回家了。它的翅膀受伤了。”

肯看着小鸟。“当然可以，”他说。“我可以带它回家。但我需要一个柔软的地方给它。”

金笑了。她从地上拿了一些柔软的草。她用草做了一张小床。然后肯带着小鸟爬上了树。他把小鸟放进了它的窝里。

小鸟非常开心。“谢谢你，金！谢谢你，肯！”它说。“你们是善良的朋友。”

金跳回她的宝宝身边。她感觉很好。她知道，当我们帮助别人时，我们也会感到快乐。

questions.question: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: A. Kangaroos can climb trees.
B. Helping others makes us happy.
C. Birds cannot fly when they are hurt.
D. Koalas are good at climbing.
questions.explanation: 故事讲述了袋鼠金帮助受伤的小鸟，最后她感到快乐，说明帮助别人会让自己快乐。

questions.question: Why can't Kim take the bird home?
choices: A. She is too busy.
B. She doesn't like the bird.
C. She cannot climb trees.
D. She is too small.
questions.explanation: 文中提到金不会爬树，而且她太大太重，所以不能把小鸟送回家。

questions.question: What can we infer about Ken?
choices: A. He is a good climber.
B. He is afraid of birds.
C. He lives in a cave.
D. He doesn't like Kim.
questions.explanation: 文中说肯住在高高的树上，而且他帮助小鸟爬上了树，可以推断他擅长爬树。

title: K — The Key in the Kitchen
text:
When Kevin found the small brass key under the kitchen table, he had no idea it would change his summer. He had been cleaning the house for his grandmother, who had recently moved to a nursing home. The key was old and slightly rusty, with a tiny tag that read "attic."

Kevin's grandmother had always been a bit mysterious. She never talked about the attic, and Kevin had never been up there. His curiosity grew as he held the key. "Maybe it's just a storage room," he thought. But why lock it?

That afternoon, Kevin climbed the narrow stairs to the attic door. The key fit perfectly. The door creaked open, and dust danced in the sunlight. The attic was full of old boxes, furniture, and a strange, musty smell. In the corner, he noticed a large wooden chest. It was unlocked.

Inside the chest, Kevin found a collection of letters, photographs, and a small leather notebook. The letters were from his grandfather, who had died before Kevin was born. They were written during the war, and they spoke of love, hope, and a secret garden he had planted for Kevin's grandmother.

Kevin read for hours. He learned that his grandfather had been a painter, and that the garden had been his last gift. The notebook contained sketches of flowers and trees, with notes about where to plant them. At the back, there was a map.

Kevin's heart raced. He realized the garden might still exist. The map led to a spot behind the old barn. The next morning, he took a shovel and followed the map. After an hour of digging, he hit something hard. It was a metal box.

Inside the box, he found a set of paints and a letter addressed to him. "Dear Kevin," it read, "if you are reading this, you have found my secret. I hope you will finish what I started. Plant these seeds and watch them grow. Love, Grandpa."

Kevin planted the seeds in the garden that week. By the end of the summer, the garden was full of colorful flowers. He had never met his grandfather, but he felt connected to him. The key had unlocked more than an attic; it had unlocked a family story.

Sometimes, the smallest things lead to the greatest discoveries.
translation:
当凯文在厨房桌子下发现那把小小的黄铜钥匙时，他没想到它会改变他的夏天。他一直在为最近搬到养老院的祖母打扫房子。钥匙很旧，有点生锈，上面有个小标签写着“阁楼”。

凯文的祖母总是有点神秘。她从不谈论阁楼，凯文也从未上去过。当他拿着钥匙时，好奇心越来越强。“也许只是个储藏室，”他想。但为什么要锁上呢？

那天下午，凯文爬上狭窄的楼梯来到阁楼门前。钥匙完美匹配。门吱呀一声开了，灰尘在阳光下飞舞。阁楼里堆满了旧盒子、家具，还有一股奇怪的霉味。在角落里，他注意到一个大木箱。它没锁。

在箱子里，凯文发现了一堆信件、照片和一个小皮面笔记本。信是祖父写的，祖父在凯文出生前就去世了。它们写于战争期间，讲述了爱、希望，以及他为凯文祖母种的一个秘密花园。

凯文读了好几个小时。他得知祖父曾是一名画家，花园是他最后的礼物。笔记本里有花和树的素描，还有关于在哪里种植的笔记。在背面，有一张地图。

凯文的心跳加速。他意识到花园可能还存在。地图指向旧谷仓后面的一个地方。第二天早上，他拿了一把铲子，跟着地图走。挖了一个小时后，他碰到了硬物。是一个金属盒子。

在盒子里，他发现了一套颜料和一封写给他的信。“亲爱的凯文，”信上写道，“如果你正在读这封信，你已经找到了我的秘密。我希望你能完成我开始的事。种下这些种子，看着它们生长。爱你的，祖父。”

那周，凯文在花园里种下了种子。到夏天结束时，花园里开满了五颜六色的花。他从未见过祖父，但他感到与祖父有了联系。钥匙不仅打开了阁楼，还打开了一个家族故事。

有时，最微小的事情会带来最伟大的发现。

questions.question: What did Kevin find under the kitchen table?
choices: A. A map
B. A small brass key
C. A leather notebook
D. A set of paints
questions.explanation: 细节题。文章第一段提到凯文在厨房桌子下发现了一把小小的黄铜钥匙。

questions.question: Why did Kevin go up to the attic?
choices: A. To clean it
B. To hide something
C. Because he was curious
D. Because his grandmother asked him to
questions.explanation: 推断题。文章第二段提到凯文的好奇心越来越强，所以他决定去阁楼看看。

questions.question: What did Kevin learn about his grandfather?
choices: A. He was a soldier.
B. He was a painter.
C. He was a gardener.
D. He was a writer.
questions.explanation: 细节题。文章第五段提到凯文得知祖父曾是一名画家。

title: K — The Kite and the Key
text:
The wind over the abandoned airfield was a living thing, tugging at Mara's jacket and whispering through the dry grass. In her hand, the kite—a fragile frame of bamboo and crimson silk—trembled like a captured bird. Her grandfather had built it decades ago, before the airfield closed and the world moved on. Now he was gone, and the kite was all that remained of his laughter.

Mara had found it in his attic, tucked inside a wooden box along with an old brass key. The key fit no lock in the house; she had tried every door. But taped to the key was a faded label: “For the sky.” It made no sense.

She decided to fly the kite, just once, to say goodbye. As it climbed, the crimson silk caught the sun, and for a moment the airfield seemed alive again. Then a sudden gust snatched the line from her fingers. The kite soared, dipped, and vanished beyond a row of derelict hangars.

Mara ran. She found the kite snagged on the roof of the smallest hangar, its silk torn but its frame intact. The door was rusted shut—except for a small padlock, green with age. Her heart hammered. She pulled the brass key from her pocket. It slid in and turned with a soft click.

Inside, dust motes danced in shafts of light. The hangar was empty except for a workbench, a chair, and a wall covered in photographs. Mara stepped closer. There was her grandfather, young and grinning, standing beside a glider. And beside him, a woman she didn't recognize, holding a kite identical to hers. Below the photo, in her grandfather's handwriting: “To my co-pilot, who taught me that some things are meant to be let go.”

Mara stood there for a long time. She had always thought the kite was a relic, a thing to keep. But her grandfather had kept it not to possess it, but to remember how to release it. The key wasn't for a door—it was for a memory.

She climbed onto the hangar roof and carefully freed the kite. This time, she didn't hold the line tight. She let the wind take it, higher and higher, until it was a speck of red against the grey sky. She watched until she could no longer tell the kite from the clouds.

Then she walked back to the workbench and sat down. On the wall, the photographs seemed to breathe. She took out her phone and called her mother. “Mom,” she said, “I found the hangar. I found him.”

There was a pause. “I know,” her mother said softly. “He always said you'd be the one to find the key.”

Mara smiled. The wind outside had quieted, but inside her, something had finally taken flight.
translation:
废弃机场上空的风是有生命的东西，它拉扯着玛拉的外套，在干草丛中低语。她手中那只风筝——竹架红绸的脆弱物件——像被捕获的鸟一样颤抖。那是她祖父几十年前做的，那时机场还没关闭，世界还在向前。如今他走了，风筝成了他笑声的唯一遗存。

玛拉在阁楼里发现了它，塞在一个木盒里，旁边还有一把旧铜钥匙。钥匙打不开家里任何一把锁；她试过每一扇门。但钥匙上贴着一张褪色的标签：“给天空。”这毫无道理。

她决定放一次风筝，只为告别。风筝攀升时，红绸迎着阳光，有那么一瞬间，机场仿佛又活了过来。突然一阵狂风从她指间夺走了线。风筝猛冲、下坠，消失在一排废弃机库后面。

玛拉跑了起来。她发现风筝挂在那座最小机库的屋顶上，绸面破了，但骨架完好。门锈死了——只有一把小挂锁，绿迹斑斑。她的心狂跳。她从口袋里掏出那把铜钥匙。钥匙滑进去，轻轻一拧，咔哒一声。

里面，尘埃在光柱中飞舞。机库里空荡荡的，只有一张工作台、一把椅子和一面贴满照片的墙。玛拉走近。那是她的祖父，年轻、咧嘴笑着，站在一架滑翔机旁。他身边有个她认不出的女人，手里拿着一只和她一模一样的风筝。照片下方是祖父的笔迹：“致我的副驾驶，是她教会我，有些东西注定要放手。”

玛拉在那里站了很久。她一直以为风筝是遗物，是拿来保存的东西。但祖父留着它，不是为了占有，而是为了记住如何放手。那把钥匙不是开门的——它是开记忆的。

她爬上机库屋顶，小心地解开风筝。这一次，她没有把线攥紧。她让风带走它，越来越高，直到它成为灰色天空中的一个红点。她一直看着，直到分不清风筝和云。

然后她走回工作台，坐下。墙上，那些照片仿佛在呼吸。她掏出手机，打给母亲。“妈，”她说，“我找到机库了。我找到他了。”

沉默片刻。“我知道，”母亲轻声说，“他总说，你会是那个找到钥匙的人。”

玛拉笑了。外面的风已经安静下来，但在她心里，有什么东西终于飞了起来。

脆弱的；易碎的（文中形容风筝的材质）
废弃的；破败的（文中形容机库）
被钩住；被缠住（文中指风筝挂在屋顶上）
挂锁（文中指机库门上的小锁）
尘埃微粒（文中指光柱中飞舞的灰尘）
遗物；遗存（文中指玛拉最初对风筝的看法）
占有；拥有（文中指把东西据为己有）
释放；放手（文中指让风筝飞走，也指情感上的释怀）
起飞；飞起来（文中比喻内心某种情感或领悟的腾飞）

questions.question: What did Mara initially believe the brass key was for?
choices: A. A door in her grandfather's house
B. A box in the attic
C. A padlock on the hangar
D. A car her grandfather owned
questions.explanation: 细节题。文中提到“The key fit no lock in the house; she had tried every door.”，说明玛拉最初以为钥匙是开家里的门的，但试了所有门都打不开。B项错误，钥匙是在盒子里发现的，不是开盒子的；C项是后来才发现的；D项文中未提及。

questions.question: Why did the grandfather keep the kite according to the story?
choices: A. To sell it for money
B. To remember how to let things go
C. To give it to the woman in the photo
D. To use it as a decoration
questions.explanation: 推断题。文中写道“her grandfather had kept it not to possess it, but to remember how to release it.”，说明祖父保留风筝不是为了占有，而是为了记住如何放手。A、C、D项均无依据。

questions.question: What does the ending suggest about Mara's feelings?
choices: A. She feels angry and betrayed
B. She feels confused and lost
C. She feels a sense of peace and connection
D. She feels determined to find the woman in the photo

title: L — The Lost Key and the Lemon Tree
text:
Lily lives in a small house near a lemon tree. She is eight years old. She loves lemons. Every morning, she picks one lemon for her mother. Her mother makes lemon water. It is cool and sweet.

One day, Lily's mother gives her a small key. "This key opens the old box in the garden," she says. "Be careful. Don't lose it."

Lily puts the key in her pocket. She goes out to play. She runs, jumps, and climbs the lemon tree. Then she looks for the key. It is not in her pocket! She is very sad.

She looks in the grass. She looks under the tree. She looks near the door. No key. Her eyes are wet. "Mom will be angry," she thinks.

Then she sees her little dog, Lucky. Lucky is playing with something. Lily goes to him. The key is in his mouth! "Lucky, give me the key!" she says. Lucky runs away. He thinks it is a game.

Lily runs after him. They run around the lemon tree. They run to the garden. They run back to the house. Finally, Lucky stops. He is tired. Lily takes the key from his mouth. "Thank you, Lucky," she says. She laughs.

Lily opens the old box with the key. Inside, there are many seeds. Her mother says, "These are lemon seeds. We can plant them. In a few years, we will have more lemon trees."

Lily smiles. She plants the seeds with her mother. Every day, she gives them water. She waits. One day, small green leaves come out of the soil. Lily is very happy.

Now Lily has many lemon trees. She still picks one lemon every morning. But she never puts the key in her pocket again. She puts it in a safe place. And she always plays with Lucky near the lemon tree.
translation:
莉莉住在一棵柠檬树附近的小房子里。她八岁。她很喜欢柠檬。每天早上，她为妈妈摘一个柠檬。妈妈做柠檬水。它清凉又甜蜜。

一天，莉莉的妈妈给她一把小钥匙。“这把钥匙能打开花园里的旧盒子，”她说。“小心点。别弄丢了。”

莉莉把钥匙放在口袋里。她出去玩。她跑、跳、爬柠檬树。然后她找钥匙。它不在她的口袋里！她非常难过。

她在草丛里找。她在树下找。她在门附近找。没有钥匙。她的眼睛湿了。“妈妈会生气的，”她想。

然后她看见她的小狗幸运。幸运正在玩什么东西。莉莉走向他。钥匙在他的嘴里！“幸运，把钥匙给我！”她说。幸运跑开了。他以为这是一个游戏。

莉莉追着他跑。他们绕着柠檬树跑。他们跑到花园。他们跑回房子。最后，幸运停下来。他累了。莉莉从他嘴里拿过钥匙。“谢谢你，幸运，”她说。她笑了。

莉莉用钥匙打开旧盒子。里面有许多种子。她的妈妈说：“这些是柠檬种子。我们可以种下它们。几年后，我们会有更多的柠檬树。”

莉莉笑了。她和妈妈一起种下种子。每天，她给它们浇水。她等待着。一天，小绿叶从土里冒出来。莉莉非常高兴。

现在莉莉有许多柠檬树。她仍然每天早上摘一个柠檬。但她再也不把钥匙放在口袋里了。她把它放在一个安全的地方。而且她总是在柠檬树附近和幸运一起玩。

questions.question: What does Lily's mother give her?
choices: A. A lemon
B. A small key
C. A dog
D. A box
questions.explanation: 故事中提到妈妈给莉莉一把小钥匙，用来打开花园里的旧盒子。

questions.question: Where does Lily find the key?
choices: A. In the grass
B. Under the tree
C. In Lucky's mouth
D. Near the door
questions.explanation: 莉莉在草丛、树下和门附近都找过，最后发现钥匙在小狗幸运的嘴里。

questions.question: What does Lily learn from the story?
choices: A. Dogs are not good pets.
B. Lemons are hard to grow.
C. Keys should be kept in a safe place.
D. Mothers are always angry.
questions.explanation: 故事结尾莉莉不再把钥匙放在口袋里，而是放在安全的地方，说明她学会了要保管好钥匙。

title: L — The Library's Lost Ledger
text:
Lena had always loved the old library in her town. Its tall shelves were filled with stories, and the smell of paper made her feel calm. But one rainy afternoon, she discovered something that changed her quiet routine.

While helping Mrs. Chen, the librarian, Lena was asked to clean the back room. There, behind a broken clock, she found a dusty leather ledger. Its pages were yellow, and the handwriting was elegant but fading. The first entry was dated 1953. It listed books borrowed by people whose names Lena had never heard.

"Mrs. Chen, what is this?" Lena asked.

The old librarian's eyes widened. "That is the lost ledger. It disappeared before I was born. People said it was thrown away when the library was repaired."

Lena turned the pages carefully. She noticed that many books had never been returned. Some were marked "overdue" in red ink. Then she saw a name that made her stop: "Arthur Lin."

"Arthur Lin?" Lena said. "That was my grandfather's name."

Mrs. Chen looked at the page. "He borrowed 'The Lighthouse at the End of the World' in 1954. It was never returned."

Lena felt a strange mix of shame and curiosity. Her grandfather had died before she was born, and her family rarely spoke about him. She decided to find out the truth.

That evening, Lena asked her mother about Grandpa Arthur. Her mother was surprised. "He loved reading," she said. "But he became ill and could not leave the house. He often asked my mother to return his books, but she was too busy with work."

Lena realized that the overdue book might still be somewhere in their attic. The next morning, she searched through old boxes. After an hour, she found a small wooden chest. Inside was a book with a dark blue cover. The title was exactly the same. On the first page, her grandfather had written: "To my dear daughter, may you always find light in stories."

Lena brought the book back to the library. Mrs. Chen was deeply moved. "You have returned more than a book," she said. "You have returned a piece of history."

Lena smiled. She understood that libraries do not only keep books; they keep memories, and sometimes they help us find what we have lost.
translation:
莉娜一直喜欢她小镇上的那座老图书馆。高高的书架上摆满了故事，纸张的气味让她感到平静。但一个下雨的下午，她发现了一件改变她平静日常的事。

在帮图书管理员陈太太打扫后屋时，莉娜被要求清理后面的房间。在那里，一个坏掉的钟后面，她发现了一本布满灰尘的皮面账簿。书页泛黄，字迹优雅但正在褪色。第一条记录日期是1953年。上面列出了莉娜从未听过的人名借阅的书。

“陈太太，这是什么？”莉娜问。

老图书管理员睁大了眼睛。“那是遗失的账簿。在我出生前它就消失了。人们说图书馆修缮时它被扔掉了。”

莉娜小心地翻着书页。她注意到很多书从未归还。有些用红墨水标着“逾期”。然后她看到一个让她停下来的名字：“亚瑟·林”。

“亚瑟·林？”莉娜说。“那是我祖父的名字。”

陈太太看着那页。“他在1954年借了《世界尽头的灯塔》。它从未被归还。”

莉娜感到一种奇怪的羞愧和好奇交织在一起。她的祖父在她出生前就去世了，家人很少谈论他。她决定查明真相。

那天晚上，莉娜向母亲询问祖父亚瑟的事。母亲很惊讶。“他热爱阅读，”她说。“但他病了，不能离开家。他经常让我母亲去还书，但她工作太忙了。”

莉娜意识到那本逾期的书可能还在他们家的阁楼里。第二天早上，她在旧箱子里翻找。一个小时后，她找到了一个小木箱。里面是一本深蓝色封面的书。书名完全相同。在第一页上，她的祖父写道：“给我亲爱的女儿，愿你永远在故事中找到光明。”

莉娜把书带回了图书馆。陈太太深受感动。“你归还的不只是一本书，”她说。“你归还了一段历史。”

莉娜笑了。她明白图书馆不仅保存书籍；它们保存记忆，有时它们帮助我们找到我们失去的东西。

vocabulary.meaning: 账簿；记录本（文中指图书馆的借阅记录本）
优雅的；漂亮的（文中形容字迹）
褪色的；逐渐消失的（文中指字迹变淡）
逾期的；过期的（文中指书未按时归还）

箱子；柜子（文中指装书的小木箱）

常规；日常（文中指莉娜平静的日常生活）
消失；不见了（文中指账簿失踪）

questions.question: Why had Arthur Lin never returned the book?
choices: A. He lost the book in the attic.
B. He became ill and could not leave the house, and his wife was too busy to return it.
C. He moved to another town and forgot about it.
D. He did not like the book and threw it away.
questions.explanation: 文中提到祖父生病不能出门，他让莉娜的祖母去还书，但她工作太忙。因此选B。

questions.question: What can we infer about Lena at the end of the story?
choices: A. She decides to become a librarian.
B. She feels angry with her grandfather.
C. She understands the deeper value of libraries and family memories.

title: L — The Lighthouse Keeper's Last Light
text:
For thirty-seven years, Elias had kept the lighthouse on Cape Wrath, and for thirty-seven years the light had never failed. The lamp was his companion, its steady beam slicing through the blackness of the Atlantic like a promise. He knew every creak of the tower, every rusted bolt, every gust that rattled the glass. The sea was his only neighbor, and he had grown to love its indifference.

But tonight was different. The lighthouse had been automated. A new electric system, installed by men with clipboards and cheerful voices, would take over at midnight. Elias had been offered a pension and a small apartment in the village. He had accepted, though his hand had trembled when he signed the papers.

He climbed the spiral staircase one last time, his knees aching, the lantern swinging in his grip. The lamp room smelled of oil and salt, as it always had. He ran his fingers over the brass railing, polished by decades of his touch. Outside, the wind howled, and the waves crashed against the rocks below, as if the ocean itself was protesting.

"You don't have to go," whispered a voice.

Elias turned. A young woman stood in the doorway, her dark hair whipped by the wind. She wore a faded yellow raincoat, and her eyes held a strange familiarity.

"Who are you?" Elias asked, his voice rough.

"I'm the one you saved," she said. "Twenty years ago, a storm. My father's boat was sinking. You kept the light burning through the night, and we found our way home."

Elias remembered. The storm had been monstrous. He had stayed awake for forty hours, feeding the lamp oil, praying that the little flame would not die. He had never known who the survivors were.

"I never thanked you," the woman said. "My father passed away last year. He told me to find you."

Elias felt a lump in his throat. "It was my duty."

"No," she said softly. "It was your heart."

They stood in silence as the clock ticked toward midnight. The new electric light flickered on, bright and cold, casting a harsh white glow over the sea. Elias watched it for a long moment, then turned away.

"Will you come down?" the woman asked.

Elias took one last look at the lamp, the old friend he was leaving behind. Then he nodded. "Yes. The light will keep shining. It doesn't need me anymore."

As they descended the stairs, Elias realized that he had not been keeping the light for the ships. He had been keeping it for himself, a beacon against his own loneliness. And now, in the warmth of a stranger's gratitude, he found a different kind of light.

At the bottom of the tower, the woman handed him a small brass key. "This was my father's. He said you might need it."

Elias turned the key over in his palm. It was old and worn, like him. He smiled, the first genuine smile in years.

"Thank you," he said. "I think I will."

And as they walked away from the lighthouse, the beam behind them swept across the water, steady and sure, no longer his burden but his legacy.
translation:
三十七年来，伊莱亚斯一直守护着愤怒角上的灯塔，三十七年来，那盏灯从未熄灭。那盏灯是他的伙伴，它稳定的光束划破大西洋的黑暗，像一个承诺。他熟悉塔楼的每一声吱呀，每一颗生锈的螺栓，每一阵吹得玻璃咯咯响的狂风。大海是他唯一的邻居，而他早已爱上它的冷漠。

但今晚不同。灯塔已经自动化了。一套新的电力系统，由那些拿着写字板和欢快声音的人安装，将在午夜接管。伊莱亚斯得到了一笔养老金和村里的一间小公寓。他接受了，尽管签字时手在颤抖。

他最后一次爬上螺旋楼梯，膝盖作痛，提灯在手中摇晃。灯室散发着油和盐的味道，一如既往。他的手指抚过黄铜栏杆，那是他数十年触摸磨亮的。外面，风在呼啸，海浪拍打着下面的岩石，仿佛海洋本身在抗议。

“你不必走，”一个声音低语道。

伊莱亚斯转过身。一个年轻女子站在门口，黑发被风吹乱。她穿着一件褪色的黄色雨衣，眼神中带着一种奇怪的熟悉感。

“你是谁？”伊莱亚斯问道，声音沙哑。

“我是你救过的人，”她说。“二十年前，一场风暴。我父亲的船正在下沉。你整夜让灯亮着，我们才找到了回家的路。”

伊莱亚斯想起来了。那场风暴极其可怕。他连续四十个小时没合眼，给灯添油，祈祷那小小的火焰不要熄灭。他一直不知道幸存者是谁。

“我从未感谢过你，”女人说。“我父亲去年去世了。他让我来找你。”

伊莱亚斯喉咙哽咽。“那是我的职责。”

“不，”她轻声说。“那是你的心。”

他们沉默地站着，时钟滴答走向午夜。新的电灯闪烁亮起，明亮而冰冷，向海面投下刺眼的白光。伊莱亚斯看了它很久，然后转过身。

“你愿意下来吗？”女人问。

伊莱亚斯最后看了一眼那盏灯，他即将离开的老朋友。然后他点了点头。“是的。灯会继续亮着。它不再需要我了。”

当他们走下楼梯时，伊莱亚斯意识到，他一直以来守着的灯并不是为了船只。他是在为自己守灯，一座对抗自己孤独的灯塔。而现在，在一个陌生人感激的温暖中，他找到了另一种光。

在塔底，女人递给他一把小小的黄铜钥匙。“这是我父亲的。他说你可能需要它。”

伊莱亚斯把钥匙在掌心翻过来。它又旧又磨损，就像他一样。他笑了，这是多年来第一个真诚的微笑。

“谢谢你，”他说。“我想我会的。”

当他们离开灯塔时，身后的光束扫过水面，稳定而坚定，不再是他的负担，而是他的遗产。

vocabulary.meaning: 冷漠，漠不关心；文中指大海的冷漠无情

巨大的，可怕的；文中形容风暴极其可怕
喉咙哽咽，说不出话；文中指伊莱亚斯感动得哽咽
闪烁，忽明忽暗；文中指新电灯闪烁亮起
灯塔，指路明灯；文中比喻对抗孤独的指引之光
感激，感恩；文中指陌生女人的感激之情
遗产，遗留物；文中指灯塔成为他留下的遗产

questions.question: Why does the young woman come to see Elias?
choices: A. She wants to buy the lighthouse from him.
B. She is a reporter writing about his retirement.
C. She was sent by the government to check the new system.
D. She wants to thank him for saving her and her father twenty years ago.
questions.explanation: 女子自述二十年前风暴中，Elias整夜点灯，救了她和父亲，父亲去年去世前让她来找Elias道谢。其他选项均与原文不符。

questions.question: What does the brass key at the end most likely symbolize?

B. The key to the lighthouse's old lamp room.

title: Mia's Missing Mirror
text:
Mia is a young girl. She lives in a small town. She has a beautiful mirror. It is from her grandmother. Mia loves her mirror very much. She looks in it every day.

One morning, Mia cannot find her mirror. She looks in her room. She looks under the bed. She looks in her bag. The mirror is not there. Mia is very sad. She asks her mother, "Mom, do you see my mirror?" Her mother says, "No, I don't. But don't worry. Let's look together."

Mia and her mother look in the kitchen. They look in the living room. They look in the garden. They cannot find it. Mia starts to cry. "It is from Grandma," she says. "I want it back."

Just then, Mia's little brother, Tom, comes in. He has something in his hand. It is Mia's mirror! Tom says, "I am sorry, Mia. I took it this morning. I wanted to see my face. I forgot to put it back."

Mia is happy to see her mirror. She says, "It's okay, Tom. But next time, please ask me first." Tom says, "I will. I am sorry." Mia smiles and gives Tom a hug. She looks in her mirror and sees her happy face.

From that day, Mia keeps her mirror in a safe place. She also lets Tom look in it sometimes. They are good friends.
translation:
米娅是一个年轻女孩。她住在一个小镇上。她有一面漂亮的镜子。这是她祖母给的。米娅非常喜欢她的镜子。她每天都照镜子。

一天早上，米娅找不到她的镜子了。她在房间里找。她在床下找。她在包里找。镜子不在那里。米娅非常伤心。她问妈妈：“妈妈，你看到我的镜子了吗？”她妈妈说：“不，我没有看到。但别担心。我们一起找吧。”

米娅和妈妈在厨房找。她们在客厅找。她们在花园找。她们找不到。米娅开始哭。“这是祖母给的，”她说。“我想拿回它。”

就在这时，米娅的小弟弟汤姆进来了。他手里拿着东西。是米娅的镜子！汤姆说：“对不起，米娅。我今天早上拿了它。我想看看我的脸。我忘了放回去。”

米娅看到她的镜子很高兴。她说：“没关系，汤姆。但下次，请先问我。”汤姆说：“我会的。对不起。”米娅笑了，给了汤姆一个拥抱。她照镜子，看到了自己快乐的脸。

从那天起，米娅把镜子放在一个安全的地方。她也让汤姆有时照照镜子。他们是好朋友。

questions.question: Where is Mia's mirror from?
choices: A. Her mother.
B. Her grandmother.
C. Her brother.
D. Her friend.
questions.explanation: 细节题。文章第一段提到“It is from her grandmother.”，所以镜子是祖母给的。

questions.question: Why is Mia sad in the morning?
choices: A. She cannot find her mirror.
B. She is hungry.
C. She lost her bag.
D. Her mother is angry.

questions.question: What does Tom do with the mirror?
choices: A. He hides it in the garden.
B. He gives it to his mother.
C. He takes it to see his face.
D. He breaks it.

title: M — The Mirror of the Mind
text:
In a small town, there was a museum that few people visited. It was old and quiet, and the only person who worked there was Mr. Chen, a man in his sixties who had spent his whole life among broken pots and dusty paintings.

One rainy afternoon, a young girl named Lily came in. She had lost her parents in an accident two years before, and she had stopped talking to anyone except her grandmother. While walking through the silent halls, she noticed a mirror in the corner. It was not like other mirrors. Its frame was made of dark wood, and strange words were carved into it.

"What does it say?" Lily asked.

Mr. Chen smiled. "It says: 'The mirror shows not your face, but your heart.'"

Lily looked into the mirror. At first, she saw only herself—a thin girl with sad eyes. But then the glass seemed to move. She saw her mother smiling at her, and her father teaching her how to ride a bike. Tears filled her eyes.

"Why do I see them?" she whispered.

"Because you have not let them go," Mr. Chen said softly. "But look again."

Lily looked once more. This time, she saw her grandmother sitting alone at home, waiting for her. She saw her classmates laughing together, and she saw herself standing outside, watching them.

"The mirror doesn't lie," Mr. Chen said. "It shows what we truly feel. You have been holding onto sadness because you are afraid to forget. But forgetting is not the same as letting go. You can keep their love in your heart and still live your own life."

Lily was silent for a long time. Then she asked, "Can I come back tomorrow?"

"Of course," Mr. Chen said. "But I hope you will also visit other places."

The next day, Lily came back—not to the museum, but to school. She sat with her classmates and, for the first time in two years, she laughed. That evening, she told her grandmother about the mirror. Her grandmother held her hand and said, "That mirror didn't change you, Lily. You changed yourself."

Lily never saw the mirror again. Years later, when she became a teacher, she often told her students the story. "There is a mirror in everyone's heart," she would say. "It shows you who you are. But only you can decide who you want to become."
translation:
在一个小镇上，有一座很少有人参观的博物馆。它又旧又安静，唯一在那里工作的人是陈先生，一位六十多岁的老人，一生都在破碎的陶罐和落满灰尘的画作中度过。

一个下雨的下午，一个叫莉莉的小女孩走了进来。两年前，她在一场事故中失去了父母，从那以后，除了祖母，她不再和任何人说话。当她走过寂静的展厅时，她注意到角落里有一面镜子。它和其他镜子不一样。镜框是深色木头做的，上面刻着奇怪的文字。

"上面写的是什么？"莉莉问。

陈先生笑了。"上面写着：'这面镜子照出的不是你的脸，而是你的心。'"

莉莉朝镜子里看去。起初，她只看到自己——一个眼神悲伤的瘦弱女孩。但接着，镜面似乎动了起来。她看到母亲在对自己微笑，看到父亲教她骑自行车。泪水涌上了她的眼眶。

"为什么我能看到他们？"她低声问。

"因为你还没有让他们离开，"陈先生轻轻地说，"但再看一次。"

莉莉又看了一次。这一次，她看到祖母一个人坐在家里，等着她。她看到同学们在一起欢笑，而她站在外面，看着他们。

"镜子不会说谎，"陈先生说，"它显示的是我们真正的感受。你一直抱着悲伤不放，是因为你害怕忘记。但忘记和放下并不是一回事。你可以把他们的爱留在心里，同时依然过好自己的生活。"

莉莉沉默了很久。然后她问："我明天还能来吗？"

"当然可以，"陈先生说，"但我希望你也去别的地方看看。"

第二天，莉莉回来了——不是回到博物馆，而是回到学校。她和同学们坐在一起，两年来第一次笑了。那天晚上，她把镜子的事告诉了祖母。祖母握着她的手说："那面镜子没有改变你，莉莉。是你自己改变了自己。"

莉莉再也没有见过那面镜子。多年后，当她成为一名教师时，她常常把这个故事讲给学生们听。"每个人的心里都有一面镜子，"她会说，"它让你看到你是谁。但只有你自己才能决定你想成为什么样的人。"

questions.question: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: A. Museums are good places for children to visit.
B. Mirrors can show people things that are not real.
C. Letting go of sadness helps people live their own lives.
D. Grandmothers always know what is best for children.
questions.explanation: 文章主旨是莉莉在博物馆的镜子前意识到自己一直沉浸在悲伤中，最终学会放下，重新融入生活。C 项最符合。A、B、D 都只是细节或偏离主题。

questions.question: Why did Lily stop talking to people except her grandmother?
choices: A. Because she was too shy to speak.
B. Because her parents died in an accident.
C. Because she did not like her classmates.
D. Because she was afraid of Mr. Chen.
questions.explanation: 文中明确提到：'She had lost her parents in an accident two years before, and she had stopped talking to anyone except her grandmother.' 因此答案是 B。

questions.question: What can we infer from the grandmother's words at the end?
choices: A. The mirror was magical and changed Lily.
B. Lily should thank Mr. Chen for the mirror.
C. Lily's change came from her own decision.
D. The grandmother did not believe the story.

title: M — The Mirror in the Museum
text:
The Museum of Fragmented Memory was a peculiar place, tucked away in a narrow alley where even the sunlight seemed to hesitate. Its curator, an elderly woman named Elara, had spent decades collecting objects that had lost their context: a broken pocket watch, a child's worn shoe, a letter never sent. But the centerpiece of her collection was an ornate mirror, framed in tarnished silver, which she claimed could reveal not your reflection, but your most buried regret.

Most visitors dismissed it as a gimmick. Yet on a drizzling Tuesday afternoon, a young man named Julian walked in, his coat dripping and his eyes hollow. He had come to test the mirror, though he told himself he was merely curious.

Elara greeted him with a nod. "You've come for the mirror," she said, not as a question. "It shows you what you've been avoiding. But be warned: it doesn't lie, and it doesn't comfort."

Julian stepped before the glass. At first, he saw only his own pale face. Then the image rippled, like a pond disturbed by a stone, and he was no longer in the museum. He was eight years old, standing in a hospital corridor. His mother was crying, and he was holding a paper crane he had made for his father, who was dying inside the room. But he had been too afraid to go in. He had turned away, and his father had died without seeing him.

The memory dissolved. Julian found himself on his knees, tears streaming down his face. Elara stood beside him, her hand on his shoulder. "The mirror doesn't show you the past to torture you," she said softly. "It shows you the moment you've been running from, so you can finally stop."

"But it's too late," Julian whispered. "He's gone. I can never apologize."

"Perhaps not to him," Elara replied. "But you can forgive yourself. That boy was only eight. He was terrified. You've been punishing him for years."

Julian looked up at the mirror again. This time, he saw not the hospital, but his father's face—not dying, but smiling, holding the paper crane. It was a memory he had forgotten: his father had found the crane on the bedside table after Julian had fled. A nurse had later told Julian that his father had held it until his last breath.

"He knew," Julian breathed. "He knew I was there. He knew I loved him."

Elara nodded. "The mirror shows you what you need to see. Sometimes that's a wound. Sometimes it's the healing you refused to accept."

Julian left the museum that evening, the rain having stopped. He didn't feel cured, but he felt lighter, as if he had set down a suitcase he had been carrying for decades. He realized that memory is not a cage; it is a room. You can choose to live in the dark corner, or you can open the curtains.

The mirror, Elara knew, would wait for its next visitor. It had no magic of its own. It simply reflected what people brought to it: their guilt, their longing, their refusal to let go. And sometimes, in that reflection, they found the mercy they had never granted themselves.
translation:
碎片记忆博物馆是个奇特的地方，藏匿在一条狭窄的小巷里，连阳光似乎都犹豫着是否要照进去。它的馆长是一位名叫伊拉拉的老妇人，她花了几十年收集那些失去背景的物品：一块坏掉的怀表，一只孩子穿旧的鞋，一封从未寄出的信。但她收藏的核心是一面华丽的镜子，镜框是失去光泽的银，她声称它映出的不是你的倒影，而是你最深的遗憾。

大多数游客把它当作噱头。然而在一个下着毛毛雨的周二下午，一个名叫朱利安的年轻人走了进来，他的外套滴着水，眼神空洞。他来测试那面镜子，尽管他告诉自己只是好奇。

伊拉拉向他点头致意。“你是为镜子来的，”她说，不是疑问句。“它向你展示你一直逃避的东西。但警告你：它不说谎，也不安慰人。”

朱利安走到镜子前。起初，他只看到自己苍白的脸。然后影像荡漾起来，像被石头扰动的池塘，他不再在博物馆里。他八岁，站在医院走廊里。他的母亲在哭，他拿着为父亲做的纸鹤，父亲正在房间里死去。但他太害怕了，不敢进去。他转身离开了，父亲死前没有见到他。

记忆消散了。朱利安发现自己跪在地上，泪水顺着脸颊流下。伊拉拉站在他身边，手放在他的肩上。“镜子展示过去不是为了折磨你，”她轻声说。“它展示你一直逃避的那一刻，这样你终于可以停下来。”

“但太晚了，”朱利安低声说。“他走了。我永远无法道歉。”

“也许不能对他，”伊拉拉回答。“但你可以原谅自己。那个男孩只有八岁。他吓坏了。你惩罚了他多年。”

朱利安再次抬头看镜子。这一次，他看到的不是医院，而是父亲的脸——不是垂死，而是微笑，拿着纸鹤。这是他忘记的记忆：他逃跑后，父亲在床头柜上发现了纸鹤。后来一位护士告诉朱利安，父亲一直握着它直到最后一口气。

“他知道，”朱利安呼吸急促。“他知道我在那里。他知道我爱他。”

伊拉拉点头。“镜子向你展示你需要看到的。有时是伤口。有时是你拒绝接受的治愈。”

那天晚上朱利安离开博物馆，雨已经停了。他没有感到痊愈，但感到轻松了，仿佛放下了背了几十年的行李箱。他意识到记忆不是笼子；它是一个房间。你可以选择住在黑暗的角落，或者你可以拉开窗帘。

伊拉拉知道，镜子会等待下一个访客。它本身没有魔法。它只是反映人们带给它的东西：他们的内疚，他们的渴望，他们拒绝放手。而有时，在那倒影中，他们找到了从未给予自己的慈悲。

questions.question: What is the main theme of the story?
choices: A. The importance of collecting old objects.
B. The power of forgiveness and self-acceptance.
C. The danger of magical mirrors.
D. The history of a museum.
questions.explanation: 故事通过朱利安在镜子中面对过去的遗憾，最终学会原谅自己，体现了宽恕与自我接纳的主题。A项只是背景，C项与故事主旨相反，D项过于表面。

questions.question: Why did Julian feel guilty about his father's death?
choices: A. He had not made a paper crane for his father.
B. He had been too afraid to enter the hospital room.
C. He had forgotten to visit his father.
D. He had argued with his father before he died.
questions.explanation: 文中提到朱利安八岁时站在医院走廊，因为害怕而没有走进父亲的房间，因此感到内疚。A项错误，他做了纸鹤；C、D项文中未提及。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the mirror from the last paragraph?
choices: A. It has magical powers that can change the past.
B. It only shows pleasant memories.
C. It reflects what people bring to it, helping them find mercy.
D. It is a fake and has no effect on visitors.
questions.explanation: 最后一段提到镜子本身没有魔法，只是反映人们带给它的东西，有时人们能在倒影中找到慈悲。A项错误，它不能改变过去；B项错误，它也展示痛苦记忆；D项错误，它确实对访客有影响。

title: N — The New Notebook
text:
Lily found a new notebook on her desk. It was small and blue. She looked inside. There was a name on the first page: "Tom".

Lily did not know Tom. She asked her teacher, Mrs. Wang. "Tom is a new student," Mrs. Wang said. "He is in the hospital today. He will come to school tomorrow."

Lily wanted to give the notebook back. The next day, she saw a boy in a blue jacket. "Are you Tom?" she asked. "Yes," the boy said. "Is this your notebook?" Lily asked. Tom looked at it and smiled. "Yes! Thank you!" he said.

Tom opened the notebook. "Oh no," he said. "My homework is not here. I did it last night."

Lily looked at the notebook again. "Wait," she said. "This is not your notebook. Your name is on the first page, but your homework is not inside."

Tom was surprised. "Then whose notebook is this?" he asked.

Lily thought for a moment. "Maybe it is your sister's," she said. "She has the same name."

Tom laughed. "I don't have a sister," he said. "But my cousin's name is also Tom. He is in Class 2."

They went to Class 2. A boy there had the same blue notebook. "This is mine!" he said. "Thank you!"

Tom found his notebook in his bag. "I am happy," he said. "Now I have a new friend, Lily."

Lily smiled. "Me too," she said. "And I learned a lesson: always look inside before you say it is yours."
translation:
莉莉在她的桌子上发现了一个新笔记本。它又小又蓝。她往里面看。第一页上有一个名字：“汤姆”。

莉莉不认识汤姆。她问她的老师王老师。“汤姆是一个新学生，”王老师说。“他今天在医院。他明天会来学校。”

莉莉想把笔记本还回去。第二天，她看到一个穿蓝色夹克的男孩。“你是汤姆吗？”她问。“是的，”男孩说。“这是你的笔记本吗？”莉莉问。汤姆看了看，笑了。“是的！谢谢你！”他说。

汤姆打开笔记本。“哦不，”他说。“我的作业不在这里。我昨晚做了作业。”

莉莉又看了看笔记本。“等等，”她说。“这不是你的笔记本。你的名字在第一页，但你的作业不在里面。”

汤姆很惊讶。“那这是谁的笔记本？”他问。

莉莉想了一会儿。“也许是你妹妹的，”她说。“她有同样的名字。”

汤姆笑了。“我没有妹妹，”他说。“但我表弟的名字也是汤姆。他在二班。”

他们去了二班。那里的一个男孩有同样的蓝色笔记本。“这是我的！”他说。“谢谢你！”

汤姆在他的包里找到了他的笔记本。“我很高兴，”他说。“现在我有了一个新朋友，莉莉。”

莉莉笑了。“我也是，”她说。“而且我学到了一个教训：在说它是你的之前，一定要先看看里面。”

title: N — The Notebook of Nina
text:
Nina had always been a quiet girl who preferred books to people. In her small town, everyone knew everyone, but Nina felt like a stranger. Her only comfort was a worn-out notebook where she wrote down everything she noticed: the way the sun set behind the old church, the sound of rain on the roof, the sadness in her neighbor Mr. Gable's eyes.

One afternoon, while sitting on a park bench, Nina saw Mr. Gable feeding the pigeons. He looked lonelier than ever. She had heard that his wife had passed away two years ago, and since then he rarely spoke to anyone. Nina wanted to reach out, but she didn't know how. Instead, she wrote a short poem about the pigeons and slipped it into his mailbox later that day. She didn't sign her name.

The next week, a small note appeared in Nina's own mailbox: "Thank you for the poem. It made me smile." Nina's heart leaped. She wrote back, still without signing her name. This began a secret exchange of notes between them. Through their words, Nina learned that Mr. Gable had been a teacher and loved poetry. He learned that Nina dreamed of becoming a writer but was afraid of being judged.

Months passed. One day, Mr. Gable's note said, "I'd like to meet my secret friend." Nina panicked. What if he was disappointed? But she gathered her courage and agreed to meet at the park bench.

When Mr. Gable saw Nina, his eyes widened. "You? The quiet girl from next door?" Nina nodded, blushing. Mr. Gable smiled warmly. "I should have known. Your words were always kind and observant." He then handed her a small book. "I've written down some of my own poems. I want you to have it."

Nina opened the book and found a note inside: "To Nina, the writer next door. Keep writing. Your words matter." Tears filled her eyes. She realized that her notebook had not only recorded the world but had also built a bridge to a lonely heart.

From that day on, Nina and Mr. Gable met every week to share their writing. And Nina's notebook, once a private refuge, became a place where two friends connected.
translation:
妮娜一直是个安静的女孩，比起人，她更喜欢书。在她的小镇上，每个人都认识每个人，但妮娜觉得自己像个陌生人。她唯一的安慰是一本破旧的笔记本，她在上面记下她注意到的一切：太阳落在老教堂后面的样子，雨打在屋顶上的声音，邻居盖博先生眼中的悲伤。

一个下午，妮娜坐在公园的长椅上，看见盖博先生在喂鸽子。他看起来比以往更孤独。她听说他的妻子两年前去世了，从那以后他几乎不和任何人说话。妮娜想伸出援手，但不知道怎么做。于是，她写了一首关于鸽子的短诗，当天晚些时候悄悄放进他的邮箱。她没有署名。

第二周，妮娜自己的邮箱里出现了一张小纸条：“谢谢你的诗。它让我笑了。”妮娜的心怦怦直跳。她回了信，仍然没有署名。这开始了他们之间秘密的纸条交换。通过文字，妮娜得知盖博先生曾是一名教师，热爱诗歌。他得知妮娜梦想成为作家，但害怕被人评判。

几个月过去了。一天，盖博先生的纸条上写着：“我想见见我的秘密朋友。”妮娜慌了。如果他失望怎么办？但她鼓起勇气，同意在公园的长椅上见面。

当盖博先生看到妮娜时，他的眼睛睁大了。“你？隔壁那个安静的女孩？”妮娜脸红了，点点头。盖博先生温暖地笑了。“我应该知道的。你的文字总是那么善良和善于观察。”然后他递给她一本小书。“我写下了一些自己的诗。我想送给你。”

妮娜打开书，发现里面有一张纸条：“给妮娜，隔壁的作家。继续写下去。你的文字很重要。”泪水涌上了她的眼睛。她意识到，她的笔记本不仅记录了世界，还搭建了一座通往孤独心灵的桥梁。

从那天起，妮娜和盖博先生每周见面分享他们的作品。而妮娜的笔记本，曾经是一个私人的避难所，变成了两个朋友连接的地方。

title: N — The Notebook of a Night Wanderer
text:
Nathan never intended to become a thief. He was, by all accounts, an ordinary university student—diligent, introverted, and perpetually short of money. His part-time job at a campus café barely covered his rent, let alone the textbooks he needed for his literature course. So when he found the notebook lying on a park bench one frosty November evening, he did what any desperate student might do: he picked it up, hoping to find something valuable inside.

The notebook was bound in cracked black leather, its pages yellowed with age. But what caught Nathan's attention was not its appearance—it was its content. The first page read: "Property of Eleanor Vance. If found, please return to 17 Ashwood Lane. Reward offered." Nathan hesitated. A reward? That could solve his immediate problems. But as he flipped through the pages, he forgot all about money. The notebook was filled with handwritten stories—vivid, poignant, and deeply personal. They were tales of a woman who had traveled the world, loved fiercely, and lost profoundly. Each entry was dated, and the most recent one was from just three days ago.

Nathan couldn't stop reading. He read about Eleanor's childhood in a coastal village, her tumultuous marriage to a painter, and her eventual solitude after his death. He read about her regrets, her joys, and her unwavering belief that stories could heal. By the time he reached the last page, he felt as though he knew her intimately. The final entry read: "To whoever finds this notebook—I hope my words bring you comfort. Life is fleeting, but stories endure."

Guilt gnawed at Nathan. He had planned to sell the notebook or at least claim the reward without returning it. Now, that seemed unthinkable. He looked up the address. 17 Ashwood Lane was only a twenty-minute walk from his apartment.

The next morning, Nathan stood before a modest house with a overgrown garden. He knocked, and an elderly woman answered. Her eyes were bright but tired, and she smiled warmly. "You found my notebook," she said, as if she had been expecting him. "I left it there on purpose, you know. I wanted to see if anyone would read it and care enough to return it."

Nathan was taken aback. "On purpose? But why?"

Eleanor invited him in. Over tea, she explained. She had no family left, and her health was failing. She wanted to know if her stories mattered to anyone beyond herself. "And you, young man, you read them all, didn't you?" she asked. Nathan nodded, embarrassed. "Then they matter," she said simply.

They talked for hours. Eleanor told him stories she had never written down, and Nathan shared his own dreams of becoming a writer. When he finally left, she pressed a small envelope into his hand. "For the reward," she said. Inside was not money, but a key to her study and a note: "Come back whenever you like. The stories are yours now."

Nathan did return, again and again. Over the following months, he helped Eleanor organize her manuscripts, and she became his mentor. She taught him that writing was not about fame or fortune, but about connecting with others. When Eleanor passed away peacefully the next spring, Nathan was by her side. He inherited her notebooks—dozens of them—and a mission: to ensure her stories were never forgotten.

Years later, Nathan published a collection of Eleanor's tales, along with his own. The book was titled The Night Wanderer's Legacy, and in the preface, he wrote: "I set out to steal a notebook, but I ended up finding a life."
translation:
内森从未想过要当小偷。大家都说，他是个普通的大学生——勤奋、内向，而且永远缺钱。他在校园咖啡馆的兼职勉强够付房租，更别提文学课所需的教科书了。因此，当他在一个寒冷的十一月傍晚发现公园长椅上那个笔记本时，他做了任何绝望的学生都可能做的事：他捡了起来，希望能找到什么值钱的东西。

笔记本是黑色皮革装订的，已经开裂，书页因年久而泛黄。但吸引内森的并非它的外表——而是它的内容。第一页写着：“埃莉诺·万斯的财产。若拾获，请归还至阿什伍德巷17号。有酬谢。”内森犹豫了。酬谢？那能解决他的燃眉之急。但当他翻阅书页时，他完全忘了钱的事。笔记本里写满了手写的故事——生动、辛酸，而且极其私密。它们是一个女人的故事，她曾环游世界，热烈地爱过，也深深地失去过。每篇都有日期，最近的一篇就在三天前。

内森无法停止阅读。他读到埃莉诺在沿海村庄的童年，她与一位画家的动荡婚姻，以及画家去世后她最终的孤独。他读到她的遗憾、她的欢乐，以及她坚定的信念：故事可以治愈人心。当他读到最后一页时，他觉得自己已经与她熟识。最后一篇写道：“致发现这个笔记本的人——希望我的文字能带给你安慰。生命短暂，但故事长存。”

内森感到愧疚啃噬着他。他本打算卖掉笔记本，或者至少不归还就领取酬谢。现在，那似乎不可想象。他查了地址。阿什伍德巷17号离他的公寓只有二十分钟的步行路程。

第二天早上，内森站在一栋简朴的房子前，花园杂草丛生。他敲了敲门，一位老妇人应了门。她的眼睛明亮但疲惫，她热情地微笑。“你找到了我的笔记本，”她说，仿佛她一直在等他。“你知道，我是故意把它留在那里的。我想看看是否有人会读它，并且在乎到把它还回来。”

内森吃了一惊。“故意？但为什么？”

埃莉诺请他进屋。喝茶时，她解释道。她已经没有家人了，健康也在衰退。她想知道她的故事是否对除她自己以外的任何人有意义。“而你，年轻人，你全都读完了，对吧？”她问。内森点了点头，有些尴尬。“那么它们就有意义，”她简单地说。

他们聊了几个小时。埃莉诺给他讲了她从未写下的故事，内森分享了自己成为作家的梦想。当他终于离开时，她把一个小信封塞到他手里。“这是酬谢，”她说。里面不是钱，而是一把通往她书房的钥匙和一张纸条：“随时回来。这些故事现在是你的了。”

内森确实回去了，一次又一次。在接下来的几个月里，他帮埃莉诺整理她的手稿，她成了他的导师。她教他，写作不是为了名利，而是为了与他人建立联系。当埃莉诺在第二年春天平静地去世时，内森在她身边。他继承了她的笔记本——几十本——以及一个使命：确保她的故事永远不会被遗忘。

多年后，内森出版了埃莉诺的故事集，连同他自己的。这本书名为《夜行者的遗产》，在序言中，他写道：“我本打算偷一个笔记本，却最终找到了一种人生。”

title: On the Old Oak Tree
text:
Ollie is a small owl. He lives in a big old oak tree. Every night, he sits on a branch and looks at the moon. He wants to fly far away.

One evening, Ollie sees a bright light in the sky. It is a big balloon. The balloon comes down and stops near his tree. A man gets out. "Hello, little owl! My name is Ben. Do you want to come with me?"

Ollie is very happy. He jumps into the basket. The balloon goes up, up, up. Ollie can see the river, the hills, and many small houses. "This is great!" he says.

But then the wind stops. The balloon does not move. It stays in one place for a long time. Ben looks worried. "We need wind to go home," he says.

Ollie looks down. He sees his old oak tree. It looks so small now. He also sees his family. They are flying around the tree. They look up at him. Ollie feels sad. He wants to go home.

"Don't worry," says Ben. "I have some food. We can wait here. The wind will come."

They eat some bread and drink some water. Ollie tells Ben about his tree and his family. Ben tells Ollie about his home near the sea.

After a long time, the wind comes back. The balloon moves again. Ben makes it go down near the oak tree. Ollie jumps out. "Thank you, Ben!" he says.

"You are welcome," says Ben. "You are a brave little owl."

Ollie flies to his family. He is very happy. He learns something important: home is the best place in the world.
translation:
奥利是一只小猫头鹰。他住在一棵又大又老的橡树上。每天晚上，他坐在树枝上看月亮。他想飞到很远的地方。

一天傍晚，奥利看见天空中有一道亮光。那是一个大气球。气球降下来，停在他的树附近。一个男人走了出来。“你好，小猫头鹰！我叫本。你想和我一起去吗？”

奥利非常高兴。他跳进篮子里。气球升啊升，升得高高的。奥利能看到河流、山丘和许多小房子。“这太棒了！”他说。

但后来风停了。气球不动了。它在一个地方停了很久。本看起来很担心。“我们需要风才能回家，”他说。

奥利往下看。他看见了他的老橡树。它现在看起来那么小。他还看见了他的家人。他们正绕着树飞。他们抬头看着他。奥利感到难过。他想回家。

“别担心，”本说。“我有一些食物。我们可以在这里等。风会来的。”

他们吃了一些面包，喝了一些水。奥利给本讲他的树和他的家人。本给奥利讲他海边附近的家。

过了很长时间，风回来了。气球又动了。本让气球降落在橡树附近。奥利跳了出来。“谢谢你，本！”他说。

“不客气，”本说。“你是一只勇敢的小猫头鹰。”

奥利飞向他的家人。他非常开心。他学到了重要的一件事：家是世界上最好的地方。
