title: O — The Orchestra's Missing Oboe
titleZh: 管弦乐队失踪的双簧管
text:
Lena had been playing the oboe for six years, but she had never felt more nervous than on the morning of the city orchestra's final rehearsal. The concert was only two days away, and the solo piece she had practiced for months was the highlight of the program. As she opened her instrument case, her heart stopped. The oboe was gone.

She searched everywhere—under the chairs, behind the music stands, even in the conductor's office. Nothing. The other musicians began to arrive, and soon everyone was whispering. "Someone must have taken it," said Daniel, the first violinist. "Who would do such a thing?" Lena felt tears in her eyes. Without her oboe, the concert would be ruined.

Just then, an old man carrying a black case walked in. He introduced himself as Mr. Harper, the orchestra's former oboist who had retired ten years ago. "I heard about your problem," he said. "I still have my old oboe. It's not perfect, but it might help." Lena hesitated. She had never played another person's instrument before. But she had no choice.

During the rehearsal, Lena struggled. The keys felt stiff, and the sound was not as warm as her own oboe's. Yet, as the music flowed, something surprising happened. The old oboe seemed to have a voice of its own—a rich, slightly rough tone that blended beautifully with the strings and the horns. The conductor stopped the orchestra and smiled. "Lena, that was the best I've ever heard from you," he said.

After the rehearsal, Mr. Harper told her a story. Years ago, he had lost his own oboe on the day of a big concert. A kind stranger had lent him one, and that act of generosity had changed his life. "Now it's my turn to pass it on," he said.

On the night of the concert, Lena played the old oboe. The audience sat in complete silence, and when the last note faded, they stood and clapped for a long time. Lena realized that the instrument didn't matter as much as she had thought. What mattered was the music, and the people who shared it.

After the concert, she returned the oboe to Mr. Harper. "Keep it," he said. "One day, you'll lend it to someone else." Lena smiled, knowing that the story would continue.
translation:
莉娜已经吹了六年双簧管，但在市管弦乐队最后一次排练的那个早晨，她从未感到如此紧张。音乐会只剩两天了，而她练习了数月的独奏曲目是整场演出的亮点。当她打开乐器盒时，她的心跳几乎停止。双簧管不见了。

她到处寻找——椅子下面、谱架后面，甚至指挥的办公室。什么都没有。其他乐手陆续到达，很快每个人都在窃窃私语。“一定有人拿走了它，”第一小提琴手丹尼尔说。“谁会做这种事？”莉娜感到眼泪在眼眶里打转。没有双簧管，音乐会就毁了。

就在这时，一位提着黑色箱子的老人走了进来。他自我介绍叫哈珀先生，是十年前退休的乐队前双簧管手。“我听说了你的问题，”他说。“我还留着我旧的双簧管。它不完美，但也许能帮上忙。”莉娜犹豫了。她以前从未吹过别人的乐器。但她别无选择。

排练期间，莉娜很吃力。按键感觉很僵硬，音色也不如她自己的双簧管温暖。然而，随着音乐流淌，一件令人惊讶的事情发生了。这支旧双簧管似乎有它自己的声音——一种丰富、略带粗犷的音色，与弦乐和圆号美妙地融合在一起。指挥停下乐队，微笑着说：“莉娜，这是我听过你演奏得最好的一次。”

排练结束后，哈珀先生给她讲了一个故事。多年前，他在一场大型音乐会当天丢了自己的双簧管。一位好心的陌生人借给了他一支，而那个慷慨之举改变了他的一生。“现在轮到我把它传递下去了，”他说。

音乐会当晚，莉娜演奏了那支旧双簧管。观众鸦雀无声，当最后一个音符消散时，他们站起来长时间地鼓掌。莉娜意识到，乐器并没有她想象的那么重要。重要的是音乐，以及分享音乐的人们。

音乐会结束后，她把双簧管还给了哈珀先生。“留着吧，”他说。“总有一天，你会把它借给别人的。”莉娜笑了，她知道这个故事还会继续。

questions.question: Why was Lena so nervous on the morning of the rehearsal?
choices: A. She had never played in an orchestra before.
B. Her oboe was missing before an important concert.
C. The conductor had asked her to play a solo without practice.
D. She had lost the music score for the solo piece.
questions.explanation: 细节题。文章第一段明确提到，音乐会只剩两天，她打开乐器盒时发现双簧管不见了，因此非常紧张。A、C、D均未在文中提及。

questions.question: What surprised Lena during the rehearsal with Mr. Harper's oboe?
choices: A. The old oboe was easier to play than her own.
B. The conductor did not notice the difference.
C. The old oboe had a unique tone that blended beautifully.
D. Mr. Harper asked her to return the oboe immediately.
questions.explanation: 细节题。第四段提到，旧双簧管有自己独特的音色——丰富、略带粗犷，与弦乐和圆号美妙融合，指挥也称赞了她。A与原文相反；B、D未提及。

questions.question: What is the main message of the story?
choices: A. Old instruments are always better than new ones.
B. It is important to practice before a concert.
C. Music is about sharing and generosity, not the instrument itself.
D. Never lend your instrument to someone else.
questions.explanation: 主旨题。文章结尾莉娜意识到乐器并不那么重要，重要的是音乐和分享音乐的人；哈珀先生的故事也强调了慷慨传递。A过于绝对；B不是核心；D与文章主题相反。

title: O — The Owl Who Overheard
text:
In the ancient orchard at the edge of the village, an old owl named Orion had a reputation for silence. He would perch on the same gnarled branch every evening, motionless as a shadow, listening to the conversations of the villagers who strolled beneath his tree. They never noticed him, or if they did, they dismissed him as part of the scenery. But Orion overheard everything—secrets, joys, and the quiet sorrows that people only confessed under the cover of dusk.

One autumn evening, a young woman named Elara came to the orchard with a heavy heart. She sat on a wooden bench, her hands trembling as she clutched a letter. "I cannot do it," she whispered to the empty air. "I cannot leave my father alone. But if I stay, I will never become the musician I dream of being." Orion tilted his head. He had heard this dilemma before, in different words, from different mouths. The orchard was full of such crossroads.

The next day, Elara returned with her father, a stooped man with kind eyes. "You should go," he said softly. "I have heard you play. The world needs your music more than I need your company." Elara shook her head, tears welling up. "But who will look after you?" Her father smiled. "I have the orchard, and the orchard has its guardian." He glanced up at Orion, who blinked once, slowly, as if to say, I am here.

Elara left for the city the following week. Seasons passed. Orion watched the orchard bloom and wither, and he listened to the father's lonely footsteps. The man would often talk to the tree, telling it about Elara's letters, her first concert, her first solo. "She is happy," he would say, and his voice carried both pride and a faint echo of loss.

Then, one winter evening, a carriage stopped at the orchard's edge. Elara stepped out, her coat dusted with snow, a violin case in her hand. She had come home for a visit—but it was more than that. She had returned to stay. "I have learned something," she told her father, who embraced her with surprising strength. "Music is not only about stages and applause. It is also about the people who listen. And I want to listen to you, for a change."

Orion, from his branch, felt a warmth he could not name. He had spent years observing, never interfering, never speaking. Yet somehow, his silent presence had been a kind of reassurance—a witness to the father's patience and the daughter's courage. The orchard had been a stage for a different kind of performance: the quiet act of letting go, and the even quieter act of coming back.

As the snow fell, Orion spread his wings and flew into the night. He did not need to overhear anymore. Some stories, he realized, resolve themselves not through grand gestures, but through the simple, steady rhythm of listening—and waiting. And sometimes, the best thing you can do for someone is simply to be there, even if they never know it.
translation:
在村边的古老果园里，一只名叫俄里翁的老猫头鹰以沉默闻名。每天傍晚，他都会栖息在同一根粗糙的树枝上，像影子一样一动不动，听着树下漫步的村民们的谈话。他们从未注意到他，即使注意到了，也只当他是景物的一部分。但俄里翁偷听到了一切——秘密、欢乐，以及人们只在暮色掩护下才吐露的安静悲伤。

一个秋天的傍晚，一位名叫埃拉拉的年轻女子心情沉重地来到果园。她坐在木凳上，双手颤抖着紧握一封信。“我做不到，”她对着空气低语。“我不能丢下父亲一个人。但如果我留下，我就永远无法成为我梦想中的音乐家。”俄里翁歪了歪头。他以前听过这种两难，不同的措辞，不同的人。果园里充满了这样的十字路口。

第二天，埃拉拉带着父亲回来了，一位驼背但眼神和善的男人。“你应该去，”他轻声说。“我听过你演奏。世界比我更需要你的音乐。”埃拉拉摇摇头，泪水涌上眼眶。“但谁来照顾你？”父亲笑了。“我有果园，果园有它的守护者。”他抬头看了一眼俄里翁，后者缓缓眨了一下眼，仿佛在说：我在这儿。

埃拉拉第二周动身去了城市。季节更替。俄里翁看着果园开花又凋零，听着父亲孤独的脚步声。男人常常对着树说话，讲述埃拉拉的信、她的第一场音乐会、她的第一次独奏。“她很快乐，”他会说，声音里既有骄傲，也有一丝淡淡的失落。

然后，一个冬天的傍晚，一辆马车停在果园边。埃拉拉下了车，外套上落满了雪，手里提着小提琴盒。她回家探亲——但不止如此。她回来长住了。“我明白了一些事，”她对父亲说，父亲以惊人的力量拥抱了她。“音乐不只是舞台和掌声。它也是关于倾听的人。而我想倾听你，换一换。”

俄里翁在树枝上，感到一种说不出的温暖。他花了多年观察，从不干涉，从不说话。但不知怎的，他沉默的存在成了一种安慰——见证父亲的耐心和女儿的勇气。果园一直是一种不同表演的舞台：放手的安静举动，以及更安静的归来举动。

雪落下时，俄里翁展开翅膀，飞入夜色。他不再需要偷听了。他意识到，有些故事不是通过盛大的举动解决的，而是通过倾听和等待那简单而稳定的节奏。有时，你能为别人做的最好的事，就是简单地在那里，即使他们永远不会知道。

vocabulary.meaning: 粗糙的，扭曲的（尤指树木）

questions.question: What is the main theme of the story?
choices: A. The importance of pursuing fame and success.
B. The value of silent observation and listening.
C. The conflict between city life and country life.
D. The necessity of leaving home to find happiness.
questions.explanation: 故事通过猫头鹰俄里翁的视角，强调了默默观察和倾听的价值。A项与故事中音乐家追求舞台但最终回归家庭的转变不符；C项不是核心；D项与埃拉拉最终回家相反。

questions.question: Why did Elara return to the orchard to stay?
choices: A. She failed in the city and had no other choice.
B. She wanted to take care of her father because he was ill.
C. She realized that music is also about listening to loved ones.
D. She missed the orchard and the owl.
questions.explanation: 文中埃拉拉说：“Music is not only about stages and applause. It is also about the people who listen. And I want to listen to you, for a change.” 表明她意识到音乐也包括倾听所爱的人。A、B、D项文中未提及或不是主要原因。

questions.question: What can be inferred about Orion's role in the story?
choices: A. He actively intervened to help Elara make her decision.
B. He was a magical creature with special powers.
C. He provided a silent, comforting presence to the father.
D. He was indifferent to the humans' struggles.

title: P — The Penguin and the Piano
text:
Polly is a little penguin. She lives in a cold place. Every day, she walks to the sea and looks for fish. She is happy.

One morning, Polly finds something big and black near the ice. It looks like a big box. She touches it. It makes a sound. "Ding!" Polly is surprised. She touches it again. "Dong!" The sound is beautiful.

Polly learns to play. She pushes the white and black keys with her feet. At first, the sounds are not nice. But she practices every day. Soon, she can play a simple song. The other penguins come to listen. They are happy.

One day, a strong wind comes. The piano moves on the ice. Then it falls into the sea. Polly is sad. She sits by the water and looks at the sea.

A few days later, Polly hears a sound from the water. "Ding! Dong!" She looks down. The piano is under the water! The sound is soft but clear. Polly smiles. She jumps into the sea and swims to the piano. She plays a song for the fish. The fish come and dance.

Now Polly has two homes: the ice and the sea. She plays the piano every day. She is happy again.

Sometimes things change, but we can find new ways to be happy. Polly learns this from her piano.
translation:
波莉是一只小企鹅。她住在一个寒冷的地方。每天，她走到海边找鱼。她很快乐。

一天早晨，波莉在冰附近发现了一个又大又黑的东西。它看起来像一个大盒子。她碰了碰它。它发出了一个声音。“叮！”波莉很惊讶。她又碰了一下。“咚！”声音很美。

波莉学着弹奏。她用脚推白色和黑色的琴键。起初，声音不好听。但她每天练习。很快，她能弹一首简单的歌。其他企鹅来听。它们很快乐。

一天，一阵强风吹来。钢琴在冰上移动。然后它掉进了海里。波莉很难过。她坐在水边，看着大海。

几天后，波莉听到水里传来一个声音。“叮！咚！”她往下看。钢琴在水下！声音柔和但清晰。波莉笑了。她跳进海里，游向钢琴。她为鱼儿弹了一首歌。鱼儿游过来跳舞。

现在波莉有两个家：冰上和海里。她每天弹钢琴。她又快乐起来了。

有时事情会变化，但我们可以找到新的快乐方式。波莉从她的钢琴中学到了这一点。

questions.question: What does Polly find near the ice?
choices: A. A big fish
B. A big black piano
C. A small box
D. A white key
questions.explanation: 细节题。文中提到“Polly finds something big and black near the ice. It looks like a big box.” 后来知道是钢琴。

questions.question: Why is Polly sad one day?
choices: A. She cannot find fish.
B. The other penguins do not like her song.
C. The piano falls into the sea.
D. She loses her home.
questions.explanation: 细节题。文中说“One day, a strong wind comes. ... Then it falls into the sea. Polly is sad.” 所以钢琴掉进海里让她难过。

questions.question: What does the story teach us?
choices: A. Penguins cannot play the piano.
B. We should always stay in one place.
C. Music is only for fish.
D. We can find new ways to be happy when things change.
questions.explanation: 主旨题。故事最后说“Sometimes things change, but we can find new ways to be happy.” 这是故事要传达的道理。

title: P — The Piano in the Park
text:
Every Saturday morning, Mei walked through the park on her way to the library. She always took the same path, past the pond, the old oak tree, and the small wooden stage. But one Saturday, she noticed something new: a piano had been placed on the stage.

It was an old brown piano, clearly second-hand. A sign on it read, "Play me, I'm yours." Mei stopped and looked around. Nobody was watching. She sat down and pressed a few keys. The sound was surprisingly warm.

Mei had learned to play the piano as a child, but she had stopped after her teacher moved away. For years, she had told herself she was too busy. Now, as her fingers found an old song, she felt something she had not felt in a long time: joy.

A small crowd gathered. Among them was an elderly man with a walking stick. When Mei finished, he clapped softly and said, "You play beautifully. May I try?"

Mei stepped aside. The old man sat down and began to play a piece she didn't recognize. It was full of longing and memory. When he finished, tears were in his eyes. "I used to play in a concert hall," he said. "But after my wife died, I couldn't touch a piano. This is the first time in ten years."

Mei was deeply moved. She realized that the piano had not only given her back her music but had also given the old man back his memories. They talked for a while, and the old man, whose name was Mr. Chen, offered to teach her the piece he had played. Mei accepted happily.

From that day on, every Saturday, Mei and Mr. Chen met at the piano in the park. Sometimes they played together, sometimes they just listened to others. The piano became a meeting place for people who loved music. And Mei learned that it is never too late to rediscover a passion—and that sharing it makes it even richer.
translation:
每个星期六早上，梅都会穿过公园去图书馆。她总是走同一条路，经过池塘、老橡树和小木舞台。但有一个星期六，她注意到一件新东西：舞台上有了一架钢琴。

那是一架旧的棕色钢琴，明显是二手货。上面有个牌子写着：“弹我吧，我是你的。”梅停下来环顾四周。没人在看。她坐下来，按了几个键。声音出奇地温暖。

梅小时候学过钢琴，但老师搬走后她就停了。多年来，她一直告诉自己太忙了。现在，当她的手指找到一首老歌时，她感受到了很久没有的感觉：快乐。

一小群人围了过来。其中有一位拄着拐杖的老人。梅弹完后，他轻轻鼓掌说：“你弹得很美。我可以试试吗？”

梅让到一边。老人坐下来，开始弹一首她不认识的曲子。曲子充满了渴望和回忆。弹完后，他眼里含着泪水。“我以前在音乐厅演奏，”他说。“但妻子去世后，我碰不了钢琴。这是十年来的第一次。”

梅深受感动。她意识到钢琴不仅让她重拾音乐，也让老人重拾记忆。他们聊了一会儿，老人——名叫陈先生——提出教她他刚才弹的那首曲子。梅高兴地答应了。

从那天起，每个星期六，梅和陈先生都会在公园的钢琴旁见面。有时他们一起弹，有时只是听别人弹。钢琴成了热爱音乐的人们的聚会点。梅明白了，重新发现激情永远不会太晚——而分享它会让它更加丰富。

questions.question: What did Mei notice in the park one Saturday?
choices: A. A new pond
B. A piano on the stage
C. A sign for the library
D. A group of musicians
questions.explanation: 细节题。文章第一段明确提到“a piano had been placed on the stage”，所以选B。

questions.question: Why did Mr. Chen stop playing the piano for ten years?
choices: A. He moved to another city.
B. He lost his hearing.
C. His wife died.
D. He forgot how to play.
questions.explanation: 细节题。文中陈先生说“after my wife died, I couldn't touch a piano”，说明他因妻子去世而十年未碰钢琴，故选C。

questions.question: What is the main lesson Mei learned from the story?
choices: A. Pianos should be kept indoors.
B. Old people need more help.
C. It is never too late to rediscover a passion and share it.
D. Parks are the best places to make friends.
questions.explanation: 主旨推断题。文章结尾点明“it is never too late to rediscover a passion—and that sharing it makes it even richer”，这正是梅领悟到的道理，故选C。

title: P — The Piano in the Park
text:
The piano appeared in the park on a Tuesday morning, as if it had grown there overnight. It stood beneath the old oak tree, its black lacquer cracked and peeling, its keys yellowed with age. A hand-painted sign leaned against its side: "Play me. I'm yours for the day."

For three days, nobody touched it. Children ran past, too absorbed in their games. Adults glanced at it and quickened their pace, as if the instrument might demand something of them. The piano seemed to wait, patient and silent, a monument to forgotten melodies.

On the fourth day, a girl named Priya stopped. She was twelve, with a schoolbag too heavy for her shoulders and a frown that had become permanent since her mother's illness. She had learned piano once, years ago, before everything changed. Her fingers remembered the feel of ivory, though her mind had forgotten the notes.

She sat down. Her first attempts were clumsy, a stumbling scale that drew a few amused glances from passersby. But she persisted. Slowly, the notes began to connect, forming the hesitant outline of a song she had once loved. It was not perfect. It was not even good. But it was true, and that was enough.

An elderly man in a grey coat paused to listen. He was a retired music teacher, though Priya didn't know that. He stood at a respectful distance, his hands clasped behind his back, and let the music wash over him. When she finished, he applauded softly.

"You play with feeling," he said. "Technique can be taught. Feeling cannot."

Priya shrugged, embarrassed. "I'm not very good."

"Good is a cage," the man replied. "Don't live in it."

He walked on, leaving her with those words. She sat at the piano for a long time, not playing, just thinking. Then she began again, and this time she played for no one but herself.

Over the following weeks, the piano became a gathering place. A young man with a guitar joined her one afternoon, and they improvised a duet that made a group of teenagers stop and clap. An elderly woman sang an old folk song while Priya accompanied her, her voice trembling but true. The park, once a place of solitude, began to hum with connection.

Then, one morning, the piano was gone. No explanation, no note. Just an empty patch of grass beneath the oak tree, still flattened where its legs had stood.

Priya felt a pang of loss, sharp and unexpected. She had come to rely on that piano, on the way its keys responded to her touch, on the strangers who stopped to listen. Without it, the park felt emptier than before.

But as she stood there, she noticed something. On the grass, where the piano had been, someone had placed a small wooden bench. Carved into its back were the words: "Music lives in those who make it."

She smiled. She understood then that the piano had never been the point. It had been a catalyst, a reason for people to pause, to listen, to connect. The music had always been inside her, waiting to be played.

She sat on the bench and hummed the song she had played that first day. A man passing by with a briefcase slowed his steps, then stopped. He listened. When she finished, he said, "That's beautiful. What's it called?"

She thought for a moment. "I don't know yet," she said. "But I'm writing it."

And she was. Every day, on that bench, she composed a little more of her life, note by note, without a piano, without an audience, but with something far more important: the courage to begin.
translation:
钢琴在星期二早晨出现在公园里，仿佛一夜之间从那里长出来似的。它立在老橡树下，黑色的漆面开裂剥落，琴键因年岁而泛黄。一块手绘的牌子靠在琴侧：“弹我吧。今天我是你的。”

一连三天，无人触碰它。孩子们跑过，太专注于自己的游戏。大人们瞥一眼便加快脚步，仿佛这乐器会向他们索取什么。钢琴似乎在等待，耐心而沉默，一座被遗忘的旋律的纪念碑。

第四天，一个叫普里娅的女孩停下了。她十二岁，书包对肩膀来说太沉，眉头自母亲生病以来便一直紧锁。她曾学过钢琴，多年前，在一切改变之前。她的手指还记得象牙键的触感，尽管脑子已忘了音符。

她坐下。最初的尝试笨拙，一段踉跄的音阶引来路人几许好笑的目光。但她坚持。慢慢地，音符开始连接，形成一首她曾喜爱的歌的迟疑轮廓。它不完美。甚至不好。但它真实，那就够了。

一位穿灰大衣的老人停下聆听。他是退休音乐教师，但普里娅不知道。他站在尊重的距离外，双手背在身后，让音乐冲刷自己。她弹完时，他轻轻鼓掌。

“你弹得有感情，”他说。“技巧可以教。感情不能。”

普里娅耸耸肩，窘迫。“我弹得不好。”

“好是个笼子，”老人回答。“别住在里面。”

他继续走，留下那些话。她在钢琴前坐了很久，不弹，只是想。然后她重新开始，这一次她只为自己弹。

接下来几周，钢琴成了聚集地。一个带吉他的年轻人某天下午加入她，他们即兴合奏一曲，让一群少年停下鼓掌。一位老妇人唱歌，普里娅伴奏，她的声音颤抖但真挚。公园，曾孤独之地，开始因连接而嗡嗡作响。

然后，一天早晨，钢琴不见了。没有解释，没有留言。只有橡树下空空的草地，琴腿处仍压平。

普里娅感到一阵失落，尖锐而意外。她已依赖那钢琴，依赖琴键对她的触碰的回应，依赖停下聆听的陌生人。没有它，公园比从前更空。

但当她站在那儿，她注意到什么。草地上，钢琴曾立之处，有人放了一条小木凳。凳背上刻着：“音乐活在创造它的人心中。”

她笑了。她明白了，钢琴从来不是重点。它是催化剂，一个让人暂停、聆听、连接的理由。音乐一直在她心里，等待被弹奏。

她坐在凳上，哼起第一天弹的那首歌。一个提公文包的男人放慢脚步，然后停下。他听着。她哼完，他说：“真美。叫什么名字？”

她想了想。“还不知道，”她说。“但我在写。”

她确实在写。每天，在那条凳上，她多谱写一点自己的生活，一个音符接一个音符，没有钢琴，没有观众，却有更重要的东西：开始的勇气。

questions.question: What does the piano symbolize in the story?
choices: A. The loss of childhood dreams
B. A catalyst for human connection and self-expression
C. The burden of material possessions
D. The superiority of professional musicians
questions.explanation: 文章通过钢琴引出人与人之间的连接，以及普里娅内心音乐的表达。结尾明确点出钢琴是催化剂，音乐一直在她心里，因此B正确。A、C、D均未在文中体现。

questions.question: Why does the old man say “Good is a cage”?
choices: A. He thinks Priya is a bad pianist.
B. He wants Priya to stop playing in public.
C. He believes striving only for “good” can limit true expression.
D. He thinks technique is unimportant.
questions.explanation: 老人说“技巧可以教，感情不能”，并说“好是个笼子，别住在里面”，意在鼓励普里娅不要被“好”的标准束缚，而要自由表达感情。A、B、D均曲解其意。

questions.question: What can be inferred about Priya at the end of the story?
choices: A. She has given up playing the piano forever.
B. She has found a new piano to play.
C. She has learned to create music from within herself.
D. She has become a professional musician.
questions.explanation: 结尾普里娅坐在长凳上哼歌，并说“我在写”，说明她已不再依赖外在的钢琴，而是从内心创作音乐，故C正确。A、B、D均与结尾情节不符。

title: Quiet Quail and the Queen's Quiz
titleZh: 安静的鹌鹑与女王的测验
text:
In a small village, there lived a quiet quail. Her name was Lily. Every morning, Lily ran to the forest. She liked to sit under a big tree and watch the leaves. She did not talk much. The other birds said, "Lily, you are too quiet." Lily only smiled.

One day, the Queen came to the village. She wanted to find a smart bird. "I have a quiz," said the Queen. "The first bird to answer three questions wins a prize." All the birds were excited. They flew to the Queen's garden.

The Queen asked, "What is the tallest thing in the forest?" A parrot said, "A tree!" The Queen asked, "What is the smallest thing in the forest?" A sparrow said, "A seed!" The Queen asked, "What is the most beautiful thing in the forest?" No bird answered. The parrot looked at the tree. The sparrow looked at the seed. Lily was quiet. She looked at the sky. Then she said, "The most beautiful thing is a quiet place. It is the place where you can hear your own heart."

The Queen smiled. "You are right," she said. "You are quiet, but you see more." Lily got the prize: a small golden bell. She put it on a branch. Every day, the bell rang softly. The other birds learned to be quiet too. Sometimes, the quietest bird sees the most beautiful things.
translation:
在一个小村庄里，住着一只安静的鹌鹑。她的名字叫莉莉。每天早上，莉莉都跑到森林里。她喜欢坐在一棵大树下看树叶。她话不多。其他的鸟说：“莉莉，你太安静了。”莉莉只是微笑。

一天，女王来到了村庄。她想找一只聪明的鸟。“我有一个测验，”女王说。“第一只答对三个问题的鸟会赢得奖品。”所有的鸟都很兴奋。它们飞到女王的花园。

女王问：“森林里最高的东西是什么？”一只鹦鹉说：“一棵树！”女王问：“森林里最小的东西是什么？”一只麻雀说：“一粒种子！”女王问：“森林里最美的东西是什么？”没有鸟回答。鹦鹉看着树。麻雀看着种子。莉莉很安静。她看着天空。然后她说：“最美的东西是一个安静的地方。那是一个你能听见自己心跳的地方。”

女王笑了。“你说得对，”她说。“你很安静，但你看到的更多。”莉莉得到了奖品：一个小金铃。她把金铃挂在树枝上。每天，金铃轻轻地响。其他的鸟也学会了安静。有时候，最安静的鸟看到最美的东西。

vocabulary.meaning: 听见自己的心跳（指内心平静，能感受自己）

questions.question: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: A. Being quiet can help you see beautiful things.
B. Parrots are the smartest birds.
C. The Queen likes to ask difficult questions.
D. All birds should learn to sing.
questions.explanation: 故事主旨是：安静的人或鸟往往能发现更美的东西。文章最后一句点明了这个道理。

questions.question: What did Lily say is the most beautiful thing in the forest?
choices: A. A tall tree.
B. A small seed.
C. A quiet place where you can hear your own heart.
D. A golden bell.
questions.explanation: 细节题。文中Lily回答女王第三个问题时说：'The most beautiful thing is a quiet place. It is the place where you can hear your own heart.'

questions.question: Why did Lily win the prize?
choices: A. Because she was the loudest bird.
B. Because she answered all three questions first.
C. Because she was the Queen's favorite bird.
D. Because she saw more by being quiet.
questions.explanation: 推断题。女王说'You are quiet, but you see more.' 说明Lily因为安静而看到了更多，所以赢得了奖品。

title: Quiet in the Quarry
text:
When Uncle Robert invited me to spend the summer at his quarry, I imagined loud machines and clouds of dust. Instead, I found a strange, silent world. The quarry had been closed for years, and now it was a deep, green lake surrounded by white stone walls. "It's the quietest place I know," Uncle Robert said. "That's why I asked you here."

At first, the silence bothered me. I was used to the noise of the city—traffic, music, and the constant buzz of my phone. Here, the only sounds were birds and the wind. I felt restless and kept checking my phone, but there was no signal. "What am I supposed to do all day?" I complained.

Uncle Robert smiled. "Take the rowboat out. Just don't go near the old crane." He pointed to a rusted structure on the far side of the lake. "It's not safe."

I nodded, but curiosity pulled me. The next morning, I rowed across the lake. The water was so clear that I could see the bottom. As I approached the crane, I noticed something shiny in the shallow water—a small metal box. I reached down and pulled it out. It was locked.

Back at the cabin, Uncle Robert saw the box and his face turned pale. "Where did you find that?" he asked quietly. "Near the crane," I said. He sat down and took a deep breath. "That box belonged to my father. He worked here as a foreman. When the quarry closed, he hid it, saying it held something important. We never found it. He passed away last year."

We opened the box together. Inside was a letter and a key. The letter explained that the key opened a safe deposit box in town, containing money he had saved for my education. Tears filled Uncle Robert's eyes. "He always wanted you to go to college," he whispered.

That summer, I learned that silence isn't empty. It's full of memories and love. And sometimes, the quietest places hold the loudest secrets.
translation:
当罗伯特叔叔邀请我去他的采石场度夏时，我想象着嘈杂的机器和漫天的灰尘。然而，我发现了一个奇特而寂静的世界。采石场已经关闭多年，现在变成了一个被白色石墙环绕的深绿色湖泊。“这是我知道的最安静的地方，”罗伯特叔叔说，“这就是我请你来的原因。”

起初，寂静让我感到不安。我习惯了城市的喧嚣——交通、音乐和手机不断的嗡嗡声。在这里，唯一的声音是鸟鸣和风声。我感到烦躁，不停地查看手机，但没有信号。“我整天该做什么？”我抱怨道。

罗伯特叔叔笑了。“划船出去吧。只是别靠近那个旧起重机。”他指着湖对岸一个生锈的建筑。“不安全。”

我点点头，但好奇心驱使着我。第二天早上，我划船穿过湖面。水如此清澈，我能看到湖底。当我靠近起重机时，我注意到浅水区有东西闪闪发光——一个小金属盒子。我伸手把它捞了出来。盒子锁着。

回到小屋，罗伯特叔叔看到盒子，脸色变得苍白。“你在哪里找到的？”他轻声问道。“在起重机附近，”我说。他坐下来，深吸了一口气。“那个盒子属于我父亲。他在这里当工头。采石场关闭时，他把它藏了起来，说里面装着重要的东西。我们从未找到它。他去年去世了。”

我们一起打开了盒子。里面是一封信和一把钥匙。信上解释说，钥匙能打开镇上的一个保险箱，里面装着他为我教育存的钱。泪水充满了罗伯特叔叔的眼睛。“他一直想让你上大学，”他低声说。

那个夏天，我明白了寂静并非空无一物。它充满了回忆和爱。有时，最安静的地方藏着最响亮的秘密。

questions.question: Why did Uncle Robert invite the narrator to the quarry?
choices: A. To help him work in the quarry.
B. To enjoy the quietness of the place.
C. To find the hidden box together.
D. To teach the narrator how to row.
questions.explanation: 细节题。根据第一段，罗伯特叔叔说“这是我知道的最安静的地方”，并说“这就是我请你来的原因”，说明他邀请叙述者是为了享受那里的宁静。

questions.question: What was inside the metal box?
choices: A. A map and a compass.
B. A letter and a key.
C. Some old photographs.
D. A sum of money.
questions.explanation: 细节题。第五段明确提到“Inside was a letter and a key.”（里面是一封信和一把钥匙）。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the narrator's grandfather?
choices: A. He worked as a foreman at the quarry.
B. He hid the box because he didn't trust his son.
C. He wanted the narrator to become a foreman.
D. He lost the key to the safe deposit box.
questions.explanation: 推断题。第四段中罗伯特叔叔说“That box belonged to my father. He worked here as a foreman.”（那个盒子属于我父亲。他在这里当工头。）因此可以推断出祖父曾是采石场的工头。B、C、D项均与原文不符。

title: Q — The Quiet Quail
text:
In the heart of the bustling city, where the cacophony of traffic and the constant hum of human activity never seemed to cease, there lived a young woman named Elara. She was a graphic designer, talented and ambitious, yet she felt increasingly suffocated by the relentless noise of urban life. Her apartment, though stylish, was a cage of clamor; her office, a battlefield of ringing phones and urgent emails. Elara yearned for a sanctuary of silence, a place where she could hear her own thoughts.

One weekend, on a whim, she decided to escape to her grandmother's old cottage in the countryside. The cottage had been vacant for years, and Elara remembered it as a place of eerie quietness, filled with dusty furniture and the faint scent of lavender. She hoped to find some peace there, to recharge her creative batteries.

Upon arrival, the silence was almost overwhelming. The only sounds were the rustling of leaves and the occasional chirp of a bird. As she unlocked the door, a musty smell greeted her. She spent the afternoon cleaning, and as dusk fell, she sat on the porch, watching the sunset paint the sky in hues of orange and pink. It was then that she noticed a small quail, pecking at the ground near the garden fence. It was a plain-looking bird, with a distinctive call that sounded like 'qua-quail'. Elara smiled; it was a quaint reminder of nature's simplicity.

Over the next few days, Elara found herself looking forward to the quail's visits. She named it Quincy. The bird was shy but consistent, appearing every morning and evening. Elara began to sketch it, finding inspiration in its quiet dignity. She realized that the quail, though silent for most of the day, communicated through its gentle presence. It didn't need to shout to be noticed; it simply was.

One afternoon, as she was sketching, a sudden storm rolled in. The wind howled, and rain poured in torrents. Elara rushed inside, but she worried about Quincy. The next morning, the quail was nowhere to be seen. She searched the garden, her heart sinking. Had the storm driven it away? Or worse? She felt a pang of loss, realizing how much the little bird had come to mean to her.

Days passed, and there was no sign of Quincy. Elara's initial anxiety turned into a profound sadness. She had projected her own need for quiet companionship onto the bird, and now that it was gone, the silence of the cottage felt oppressive again. She began to question her escape; perhaps she was just running away from her problems.

Then, on the fifth day, as she was packing to leave, she heard a faint 'qua-quail' from the garden. She rushed outside, and there was Quincy, followed by a line of tiny chicks. The quail had not abandoned her; it had been nesting, protecting its young. Elara's eyes welled with tears. The quail's silence had been a shield for its family.

In that moment, Elara understood. Silence wasn't emptiness; it was a space for growth and protection. She had been seeking external quiet, but what she truly needed was to cultivate inner peace. She returned to the city, not as a fugitive from noise, but as someone who could carry tranquility within her. She kept a sketch of Quincy on her desk, a reminder that sometimes the quietest voices have the most to say.

The quail taught her that strength often lies in stillness, and that amidst life's clamor, we must find our own quiet core.
translation:
在喧嚣的城市中心，交通的嘈杂声和人类活动的持续嗡鸣似乎从未停止，住着一位名叫埃拉拉的年轻女子。她是一名平面设计师，才华横溢且雄心勃勃，但她越来越感到被城市生活无休止的噪音所窒息。她的公寓虽然时尚，却是一个喧闹的牢笼；她的办公室，是一个电话铃声和紧急邮件交织的战场。埃拉拉渴望一个安静的避难所，一个能听到自己思想的地方。

一个周末，她心血来潮，决定逃到乡下祖母的旧小屋。小屋已经空置多年，埃拉拉记得那是一个安静得令人毛骨悚然的地方，满是灰尘的家具和淡淡的薰衣草香味。她希望在那里找到一些宁静，为自己的创作充电。

到达后，寂静几乎让人难以承受。唯一的声音是树叶的沙沙声和偶尔的鸟鸣。当她打开门时，一股霉味扑面而来。她花了一下午打扫，当黄昏降临时，她坐在门廊上，看着日落将天空染成橙色和粉色。就在这时，她注意到一只小鹌鹑，在花园围栏附近啄食。这是一只相貌平平的鸟，叫声独特，听起来像‘qua-quail’。埃拉拉笑了；这是大自然简单性的古怪提醒。

在接下来的几天里，埃拉拉发现自己期待着鹌鹑的来访。她给它取名昆西。这只鸟害羞但始终如一，每天早上和晚上都会出现。埃拉拉开始画它，在它安静的尊严中找到了灵感。她意识到，鹌鹑虽然一天中大部分时间都沉默，但通过它温柔的存在进行交流。它不需要大声喊叫才能被注意到；它只是存在着。

一天下午，当她正在素描时，一场突如其来的暴风雨袭来。风呼啸着，雨倾盆而下。埃拉拉冲进屋里，但她担心昆西。第二天早上，鹌鹑不见了。她搜寻了花园，心沉了下去。暴风雨把它赶走了吗？还是更糟？她感到一阵失落，意识到这只小鸟对她来说已经变得多么重要。

几天过去了，没有昆西的踪影。埃拉拉最初的焦虑变成了深深的悲伤。她把自已对安静陪伴的需求投射到了这只鸟身上，现在它不见了，小屋的寂静再次变得压抑。她开始质疑自己的逃避；也许她只是在逃避问题。

然后，在第五天，当她正准备离开时，她听到花园里传来一声微弱的‘qua-quail’。她冲出去，昆西在那里，后面跟着一队小鸡。鹌鹑并没有抛弃她；它一直在筑巢，保护它的幼崽。埃拉拉的眼眶湿润了。鹌鹑的沉默是保护家庭的盾牌。

那一刻，埃拉拉明白了。沉默不是空虚；它是成长和保护的空间。她一直在寻求外部的安静，但她真正需要的是培养内心的平静。她回到城市，不再是一个逃避噪音的逃亡者，而是一个能在内心携带宁静的人。她把昆西的素描放在桌子上，提醒自己，有时最安静的声音有最多的话要说。

鹌鹑教会她，力量往往存在于静止中，在生活的喧嚣中，我们必须找到自己安静的核心。

vocabulary.meaning: 刺耳的嘈杂声；文中指城市中交通和人类活动的喧嚣
感到窒息；文中指被噪音压抑得喘不过气
避难所；文中指埃拉拉渴望的安静之地
怪异的，令人毛骨悚然的；文中形容小屋的安静
古怪的，奇特的；文中指鹌鹑叫声的独特
投射，寄托；文中指埃拉拉把自己的情感寄托在鹌鹑身上
压抑的；文中指寂静让人感到沉闷
培养；文中指培养内心的平静
宁静；文中指埃拉拉带回城市的内心平静
喧闹；文中指生活中的嘈杂

questions.question: What is the main theme of the story?
choices: A. The importance of escaping city life.
B. Finding inner peace in silence.
C. The dangers of storms for wildlife.
D. The value of artistic inspiration.
questions.explanation: 主旨题。故事通过埃拉拉与鹌鹑的互动，最终领悟到真正的平静来自内心，而不是外在环境的安静。

questions.question: Why did the quail disappear after the storm?
choices: A. It was scared away by Elara.
B. It was injured in the storm.
C. It was nesting and protecting its chicks.
D. It migrated to another place.
questions.explanation: 细节题。第五天鹌鹑带着小鸡出现，说明它之前是在筑巢和保护幼崽。

questions.question: What can be inferred about Elara's return to the city?
choices: A. She decided to quit her job.
B. She bought a pet quail.
C. She learned to carry tranquility within her.
D. She moved permanently to the countryside.
questions.explanation: 推断题。结尾提到她回到城市时内心带着宁静，并保留素描作为提醒，说明她学会了内在的平静。

title: Ruby and the Rainbow River
text:
Ruby is a little rabbit. She lives near a small river. The river is not very big, but it is very beautiful. Every morning, Ruby goes to the river to drink water and play.

One day, it rains in the morning. Ruby stays at home. After the rain, the sun comes out. Ruby goes out and sees a rainbow in the sky. The rainbow is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple. "How beautiful!" she says. She wants to find the end of the rainbow.

Ruby walks along the river. She meets a turtle. "Hello, Turtle. Do you know where the rainbow ends?" she asks. "No, I don't," says the Turtle. "But the river is nice today. Look!" Ruby looks at the river. The water is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple, too! "Wow! The river is a rainbow!" she says.

Ruby walks more. She meets a bird. "Hello, Bird. Do you know where the rainbow ends?" she asks. "No, I don't," says the Bird. "But listen! The river is singing today." Ruby listens. The water makes a soft sound, like a song. "The river is happy," says Ruby.

Ruby walks and walks. She is tired. She sits down near the river. An old frog comes to her. "Little rabbit, why are you tired?" he asks. "I want to find the end of the rainbow," says Ruby. The frog smiles. "The rainbow has no end," he says. "But you can find its colours in the river. Look!" Ruby looks at the river again. The colours are still there. She sees red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple in the water.

Ruby smiles. "I don't need to find the end," she says. "The rainbow is here. The river is my rainbow." She drinks some water and goes home. From that day, Ruby goes to the river every day. She is happy. She knows the rainbow is always near her.
translation:
鲁比是一只小兔子。她住在一条小河边。这条河不太大，但是非常美丽。每天早上，鲁比都去河边喝水、玩耍。

一天早上下了雨。鲁比待在家里。雨停后，太阳出来了。鲁比走出去，看见天空有一道彩虹。彩虹有红色、橙色、黄色、绿色、蓝色和紫色。“真美啊！”她说。她想找到彩虹的尽头。

鲁比沿着河走。她遇到一只乌龟。“你好，乌龟。你知道彩虹的尽头在哪里吗？”她问。“不，我不知道，”乌龟说。“但是今天河水很美。看！”鲁比看着河水。水也是红色、橙色、黄色、绿色、蓝色和紫色的！“哇！这条河就是一道彩虹！”她说。

鲁比继续走。她遇到一只鸟。“你好，小鸟。你知道彩虹的尽头在哪里吗？”她问。“不，我不知道，”小鸟说。“但是听！今天河水在唱歌。”鲁比听着。水发出轻轻的声音，像一首歌。“河水很开心，”鲁比说。

鲁比走啊走。她累了。她在河边坐下来。一只老青蛙来到她身边。“小兔子，你为什么累呀？”他问。“我想找到彩虹的尽头，”鲁比说。青蛙笑了。“彩虹没有尽头，”他说。“但是你可以在河里找到它的颜色。看！”鲁比又看着河水。那些颜色还在那里。她看见水里有红色、橙色、黄色、绿色、蓝色和紫色。

鲁比笑了。“我不需要找到尽头，”她说。“彩虹就在这里。这条河就是我的彩虹。”她喝了些水，回家了。从那天起，鲁比每天都去河边。她很开心。她知道彩虹一直在她身边。

questions.question: What does Ruby want to find at the beginning of the story?
choices: A. The end of the river
B. The end of the rainbow
C. A new home
D. Her friend Turtle
questions.explanation: 故事开头提到，雨停后鲁比看见彩虹，并说她想找到彩虹的尽头（find the end of the rainbow）。因此选B。

questions.question: What does Ruby see in the river after the rain?
choices: A. Many fish
B. A big boat
C. Rainbow colours
D. A old frog
questions.explanation: 文中说鲁比看河水时，发现水也是红色、橙色、黄色、绿色、蓝色和紫色，也就是彩虹的颜色（rainbow colours）。因此选C。

questions.question: What does Ruby learn from the old frog?
choices: A. The rainbow has no end and its colours are in the river
B. The river is very long
C. The turtle and the bird are not friendly
D. She must go home before the rain
questions.explanation: 老青蛙告诉鲁比彩虹没有尽头（The rainbow has no end），但她可以在河里找到它的颜色。鲁比因此明白彩虹就在身边。因此选A。

title: R — The River's Riddle
text:
In a small village by the river, a young girl named Maya often sat on the bank, watching the water flow. She had heard stories about the river's riddle: whoever solved it would bring good fortune to the village. But many had tried and failed.

One day, Maya decided to try. She walked along the river, asking everyone she met. An old fisherman said, "The riddle is about patience. You must wait for the right moment to catch a fish." A farmer said, "It's about hard work. The river waters our fields, and we must work hard to grow crops." A child said, "It's about play. The river is fun to swim in." Maya listened but was not satisfied.

She sat by the river again, thinking. The sun set, and the moon rose. Suddenly, she noticed something: the river never stopped, yet it was always there. It gave water to everyone, asking nothing in return. It could be calm or wild, but it always found its way to the sea.

Maya smiled. She ran back to the village and said, "I have solved the riddle! The river teaches us to be generous and persistent. It gives without expecting anything, and it never gives up on its journey. That is the secret of good fortune."

The villagers were amazed. They had been looking for a complicated answer, but the truth was simple. From that day on, they tried to live like the river: helping each other and never giving up. And indeed, the village prospered.

Maya often returned to the river, not to solve any riddle, but to remember the lesson it had taught her. The river kept flowing, whispering its wisdom to anyone who would listen.
translation:
在一个河边的小村庄里，一个名叫玛雅的年轻女孩经常坐在岸边，看着河水流淌。她听说过关于河流的谜语：谁能解开它，就能给村庄带来好运。但许多人都尝试过，却失败了。

一天，玛雅决定试一试。她沿着河走，问每一个她遇到的人。一位老渔夫说：“谜语是关于耐心的。你必须等待合适的时机才能钓到鱼。”一位农民说：“这是关于辛勤工作的。河流浇灌我们的田地，我们必须努力工作才能种出庄稼。”一个孩子说：“这是关于玩耍的。在河里游泳很有趣。”玛雅听着，但并不满意。

她又坐在河边，思考着。太阳落山了，月亮升起来了。突然，她注意到了一些事情：河流从未停止，但它始终在那里。它给每个人水，却不求任何回报。它可以是平静的，也可以是狂野的，但它总能找到通往大海的路。

玛雅笑了。她跑回村庄说：“我解开了谜语！河流教导我们要慷慨和坚持不懈。它付出而不期待任何回报，并且从不放弃它的旅程。这就是好运的秘密。”

村民们很惊讶。他们一直在寻找一个复杂的答案，但真相很简单。从那天起，他们努力像河流一样生活：互相帮助，永不放弃。果然，村庄繁荣了起来。

玛雅经常回到河边，不是为了解开任何谜语，而是为了记住它教给她的教训。河流继续流淌，向任何愿意倾听的人低语着它的智慧。

questions.question: What is the river's riddle about according to Maya?
choices: A. Patience and hard work
B. Generosity and persistence
C. Play and fun
D. Wealth and fortune
questions.explanation: 玛雅在故事结尾说河流教导我们要‘generous and persistent’，即慷慨和坚持不懈。其他选项是村民的猜测，不是玛雅的答案。

questions.question: Why were the villagers amazed by Maya's answer?
choices: A. Because Maya was very young
B. Because the answer was too difficult
C. Because they had expected a complicated answer
D. Because the river told Maya the answer
questions.explanation: 文中提到村民们一直在寻找一个复杂的答案，但真相很简单，所以当玛雅给出简单答案时他们感到惊讶。

questions.question: What can we infer about Maya from the story?
choices: A. She gave up easily.
B. She was not interested in the river.
C. She was thoughtful and observant.
D. She wanted to be famous.
questions.explanation: 玛雅通过观察和思考解开了谜语，说明她善于思考和观察。她并没有轻易放弃，也不是为了出名。

title: R — The River's Refrain
text:
The river had always sung the same refrain to Mira—a low, persistent hum that seemed to say: *Stay. Drift. Forget.* She had grown up on its banks, her childhood a blur of pebbles and dragonflies, but now, at twenty-three, the melody felt less like a lullaby and more like a cage. Every morning, she watched the water glide past her window, indifferent to her restlessness, and every evening, she returned from her dead-end job at the packaging plant to the same view, the same hum, the same unspoken question: *Is this all?*

Her father had been a river man, a ferryman who knew every eddy and current by heart. He used to say, “The river doesn’t hurry, yet it always arrives.” Mira had once found comfort in that paradox, but now it taunted her. She wanted to hurry. She wanted to arrive somewhere that wasn’t just another bend in the same old stream.

One rainy Tuesday, a stranger appeared at the plant. He was a hydrologist, sent to assess the water quality after a nearby factory had been fined for illegal dumping. His name was Leo, and he carried a notebook filled with graphs and a quiet, unassuming curiosity. Mira watched him crouch by the bank, collecting samples, his movements precise yet unhurried. When he caught her eye, he smiled. “It’s a stubborn river,” he said. “It’s been carrying our mistakes for decades, but it’s also slowly cleaning itself. Given time, it recovers.”

Something in his words lodged in her chest. *It recovers.* She had never thought of the river as resilient; to her, it was merely a backdrop to her own inertia. But Leo’s calm assurance unsettled her. That night, she couldn’t sleep. The hum outside her window seemed to shift, its refrain no longer a command but a question: *What will you do?*

The next morning, she did something she had never dared: she walked into the plant manager’s office and quit. Her hands trembled, but her voice was steady. She had no plan, only a vague yearning to see where the river went—not just the part she knew, but its source, its mouth, its entire sprawling story.

She packed a small bag and followed the water upstream. For days, she hiked along the bank, through marshes and meadows, past sleepy villages and abandoned mills. The river narrowed, then widened; it rushed through gorges and lingered in quiet pools. She met a fisherman who told her legends of the river’s origin, and an old woman who gave her bread and warned her about the rapids ahead. Each encounter chipped away at her old self, revealing something rawer, more alive.

At last, she reached the source: a modest spring bubbling up from a cleft in the rocks, almost invisible beneath ferns. It was so small—nothing like the broad, imposing river she had known. Mira knelt and touched the icy water. It was then she understood: the river’s refrain was never a cage. It was an invitation. *Stay* meant *be present*. *Drift* meant *let go*. *Forget* meant *forgive yourself*.

When she returned home weeks later, the river looked the same, but she did not. She found a job at a local conservation trust, working to protect the water she had once resented. And sometimes, in the evening, she would sit by the bank and listen. The hum was still there, but now it sounded like a promise—not a command, but a companionable whisper: *You are here. You are moving. You are free.*
translation:
那条河总是对米拉唱着同样的副歌——低沉而执着的嗡鸣，仿佛在说：*留下。漂流。遗忘。* 她在河岸边长大，童年是一片由鹅卵石和蜻蜓组成的模糊记忆。但如今，二十三岁的她，觉得这旋律不再像摇篮曲，更像一座牢笼。每天清晨，她看着河水从窗前滑过，对她的躁动无动于衷；每天傍晚，她从包装厂那份没有前途的工作回来，面对同样的风景，同样的嗡鸣，同一个未曾说出口的问题：*这就是全部吗？*

她的父亲曾是个河上人，一个渡船夫，对每一处漩涡和水流都了如指掌。他常说：“河不着急，却总能抵达。”米拉曾在这种矛盾中找到安慰，但现在它却在嘲弄她。她想着急。她想抵达某个不只是同一道旧溪流中另一个弯道的地方。

一个下雨的星期二，工厂里来了个陌生人。他是一位水文学家，被派来评估附近一家工厂因非法倾倒被罚款后的水质。他叫利奥，随身带着一本画满图表的笔记本，还有一份安静而谦逊的好奇心。米拉看着他在岸边蹲下采集样本，动作精准却不慌不忙。当他迎上她的目光时，他笑了。“这是条固执的河，”他说。“它几十年来承载着我们的错误，但也在慢慢自我净化。只要给它时间，它会恢复。”

他的话在她心里扎了根。*它会恢复。* 她从未把河流看作坚韧的；对她而言，它只是她自身惰性的背景。但利奥平静的笃定让她不安。那天晚上，她无法入睡。窗外的嗡鸣似乎变了，它的副歌不再是指令，而是一个问题：*你会怎么做？*

第二天早上，她做了从未敢做的事：她走进工厂经理的办公室，辞职了。她的手在颤抖，但声音很稳。她没有计划，只有一种模糊的渴望，想去看看河流走向何方——不只是她熟悉的那段，还有它的源头、它的入海口、它整个绵延的故事。

她收拾了一个小包，沿着水流向上游走去。几天里，她沿着河岸徒步，穿过沼泽和草地，经过沉睡的村庄和废弃的磨坊。河流时而变窄，时而变宽；它冲过峡谷，又在安静的水潭里徘徊。她遇到一个渔夫，给她讲河流起源的传说；还有一个老妇人，给了她面包，并警告她前方有急流。每一次相遇都一点点削去旧日的她，露出更原始、更鲜活的东西。

最后，她到达了源头：一个从岩石裂缝中涌出的朴素泉水，几乎隐藏在蕨类植物下面。它是那么小——完全不像她所熟知的那条宽阔而威严的河。米拉跪下来，触摸着冰冷的水。就在那时她明白了：河流的副歌从来不是牢笼。它是一种邀请。*留下*意味着*活在当下*。*漂流*意味着*放手*。*遗忘*意味着*原谅自己*。

几周后当她回到家时，河流看起来还是老样子，但她已不同。她在当地一个保护信托机构找到了工作，致力于保护她曾经怨恨的水。有时傍晚，她会坐在岸边倾听。嗡鸣仍在，但现在听起来像是一个承诺——不是命令，而是一句友好的低语：*你在这里。你在前行。你自由了。*

vocabulary.meaning: 副歌；反复出现的旋律或话语（文中指河流反复的嗡鸣）
冷漠的；不关心的（文中指河流对米拉的躁动无动于衷）
悖论；矛盾的事物（文中指父亲的话看似矛盾）
水文学家（文中指利奥的职业）
谦逊的；不装腔作势的（文中形容利奥的好奇心）
有韧性的；能恢复的（文中指河流的自我净化能力）
惰性；惯性（文中指米拉自身缺乏行动力）
渴望；向往（文中指米拉想探索河流的渴望）
蔓延的；广阔展开的（文中指河流整个绵延的故事）
友好的；适合做伴的（文中形容低语般的河流声）

questions.question: What does the river's refrain initially represent to Mira?
choices: A. A comforting lullaby that helps her sleep.
B. A cage that symbolizes her stagnant life.
C. A promise of adventure and freedom.
D. A warning about the dangers of the river.
questions.explanation: 文章第一段提到，米拉觉得河流的旋律“less like a lullaby and more like a cage”，并暗示她生活的停滞。因此B正确。A与原文相反；C和D在开头并未体现。

questions.question: Why does Leo's comment about the river disturb Mira?
choices: A. Because it reminds her of her father's death.
B. Because it suggests the river is dying.
C. Because it challenges her view of the river as merely a backdrop to her inertia.
D. Because it makes her realize she should quit her job immediately.
questions.explanation: 第四段指出，米拉从未把河流看作坚韧的，利奥的话让她不安，因为“she had never thought of the river as resilient; to her, it was merely a backdrop to her own inertia”。C准确表达此意。A、B、D均无依据。

questions.question: What does Mira ultimately understand about the river's refrain?
choices: A. It was always a command she had to obey.
B. It was an invitation to be present, let go, and forgive herself.
C. It was a meaningless sound that she should ignore.
D. It was a warning to stay away from the river.
questions.explanation: 倒数第二段明确写道：“the river’s refrain was never a cage. It was an invitation. *Stay* meant *be present*. *Drift* meant *let go*. *Forget* meant *forgive yourself*.” 因此B正确。A、C、D均与原文矛盾。

title: S — The Squirrel and the Star
text:
Sam is a little squirrel. He lives in a big tree in the park. Every morning, he runs down the tree and looks for food. He likes nuts and seeds. He is very happy.

One evening, Sam sits on a branch. He looks up at the sky. He sees many stars. They are bright and beautiful. One star is very small but very bright. Sam likes it.

Every night, Sam watches the star. He talks to it. "Hello, little star. How are you?" The star does not answer. But Sam is happy.

Winter comes. It is cold and snowy. Sam stays in his tree. He has some nuts, but not many. One day, he cannot find food. He is sad and hungry.

That night, he looks at the star. The star is still there. It shines brightly. Sam feels warm in his heart. He says, "Thank you, star. You are my friend."

The next morning, Sam goes out. He meets a bird. The bird says, "I have many seeds. Do you want some?" Sam says, "Yes, please!" The bird gives him seeds. Sam is very happy.

Sam learns a lesson. Even a small star can give hope. And a friend can come when you need one. Now, every night, Sam looks at the star and smiles.
translation:
萨姆是一只小松鼠。他住在公园里的一棵大树上。每天早上，他跑下树去找食物。他喜欢坚果和种子。他很快乐。

一天晚上，萨姆坐在树枝上。他抬头看天空。他看见许多星星。它们又亮又美。有一颗星星很小但很亮。萨姆喜欢它。

每天晚上，萨姆都看着那颗星星。他对它说话。“你好，小星星。你好吗？”星星不回答。但萨姆很开心。

冬天来了。天气寒冷，下着雪。萨姆待在他的树上。他有一些坚果，但不多。有一天，他找不到食物。他既伤心又饥饿。

那天晚上，他看着那颗星星。星星还在那里。它明亮地闪烁着。萨姆心里感到温暖。他说：“谢谢你，星星。你是我的朋友。”

第二天早上，萨姆出去了。他遇到一只鸟。鸟说：“我有许多种子。你想要一些吗？”萨姆说：“是的，请给我一些！”鸟给了他种子。萨姆非常开心。

萨姆学到了一个道理。即使是一颗小星星也能带来希望。而朋友会在你需要的时候出现。现在，每天晚上，萨姆都看着那颗星星，微笑着。

questions.question: What does Sam like to eat?
choices: A. Fish
B. Nuts and seeds
C. Apples
D. Bread
questions.explanation: 文中提到“He likes nuts and seeds.”，说明萨姆喜欢坚果和种子。

questions.question: Why is Sam sad one day in winter?
choices: A. He cannot find food.
B. He loses his star.
C. The bird takes his nuts.
D. He is cold in the tree.
questions.explanation: 文中说“One day, he cannot find food. He is sad and hungry.”，说明他找不到食物所以伤心。

questions.question: What lesson does Sam learn?
choices: A. Stars are not real friends.
B. Winter is always hard.
C. Small things can give hope and friends can help.
D. Birds are better than squirrels.
questions.explanation: 最后一段提到“Even a small star can give hope. And a friend can come when you need one.”，说明萨姆学到了小事物能带来希望，朋友会在需要时出现。

title: S — The Silent Star
text:
For as long as she could remember, Lily had loved the stars. Every clear night, she would climb onto the roof of her house and gaze at the sky. Her favorite was a bright star near the moon, which she had named 'Polaris' even though she knew it wasn't the real pole star. It was simply the brightest one she could see, and it made her feel less alone.

Lily was a quiet girl. At school, she rarely spoke unless the teacher called on her. Her classmates thought she was shy, but the truth was that she found it hard to share her thoughts. Words seemed to get stuck in her throat, and she was afraid of saying something silly. So she kept to herself and observed the world from a distance, just like she observed the stars.

One day, her science teacher, Mr. Chen, announced a project: each student had to give a five-minute presentation about a topic they loved. Lily's heart sank. She had never spoken in front of the class before. That evening, she sat on the roof as usual, staring at her star. 'If only I could be as bright and steady as you,' she whispered. The star twinkled silently, offering no advice.

Over the next two weeks, Lily prepared. She read books about stars, wrote and rewrote her script, and practiced in front of the mirror. Her hands shook every time she imagined the classroom. But she remembered how the star never hid behind clouds, no matter how dark the night was. Slowly, she began to believe that she could shine too.

The day of the presentation arrived. When Mr. Chen called her name, Lily felt her legs turn to jelly. She walked to the front, her notes trembling in her hand. For a moment, she wanted to run away. But then she looked out the window, and although it was daytime, she imagined her star shining beyond the blue sky. She took a deep breath and began to speak.

Her voice was soft at first, but as she talked about the life cycle of stars, she forgot her fear. She explained how stars are born from clouds of gas and dust, how they burn for millions of years, and how some die in spectacular explosions. Her classmates listened in surprise. They had never heard Lily say so much. When she finished, the room was silent for a second, and then everyone clapped.

Mr. Chen smiled. 'That was excellent, Lily. You really know your stars.' Lily blushed and returned to her seat. That night, she climbed onto the roof again. The star seemed brighter than ever, and she realized it had never been silent at all. It had been waiting for her to find her own voice.
translation:
从记事起，莉莉就热爱星星。每个晴朗的夜晚，她都会爬上屋顶，凝视天空。她最喜欢的是月亮旁边一颗明亮的星星，她给它起名叫“北极星”，尽管她知道那不是真正的北极星。它只是她能看见的最亮的一颗，让她感觉不那么孤单。

莉莉是个安静的女孩。在学校，除非老师点名，她很少说话。同学们以为她害羞，但事实上，她觉得很难分享自己的想法。话似乎卡在喉咙里，她害怕说傻话。所以她独来独往，从远处观察世界，就像她观察星星一样。

一天，她的科学老师陈先生宣布了一个项目：每个学生都要做一个五分钟的演讲，介绍自己喜欢的话题。莉莉的心沉了下去。她从未在全班面前说过话。那天晚上，她像往常一样坐在屋顶上，盯着她的星星。“要是我也能像你一样明亮而坚定就好了，”她低声说。星星默默地闪烁着，没有给出任何建议。

接下来的两周，莉莉准备着。她读关于星星的书，写了又改写演讲稿，还在镜子前练习。每次想象教室的场景，她的手都会发抖。但她想起那颗星星，无论夜晚多么黑暗，它从不躲在云后。慢慢地，她开始相信自己也能发光。

演讲那天到了。当陈老师叫到她的名字时，莉莉觉得自己的腿都软了。她走到前面，手里的笔记在颤抖。有那么一瞬间，她想逃跑。但接着她望向窗外，虽然是白天，她想象着她的星星在蓝天之外闪耀。她深吸一口气，开始说话。

起初她的声音很轻，但当她谈到恒星的生命周期时，她忘记了自己的恐惧。她解释了恒星如何从气体和尘埃云中诞生，如何燃烧数百万年，以及有些如何在壮观的爆炸中死亡。同学们惊讶地听着。他们从未听过莉莉说这么多话。当她结束时，教室里静了一秒，然后大家都鼓起了掌。

陈老师笑了。“太棒了，莉莉。你真的很了解星星。”莉莉脸红了，回到座位上。那天晚上，她又爬上了屋顶。那颗星星似乎比以往更亮，她意识到它从未沉默过。它一直在等待她找到自己的声音。

questions.question: Why did Lily feel lonely at school?
choices: A. She had no interest in making friends.
B. She found it difficult to express her thoughts.
C. Her classmates often laughed at her.
D. She was too busy studying stars.
questions.explanation: 细节题。第二段提到“she found it hard to share her thoughts. Words seemed to get stuck in her throat, and she was afraid of saying something silly.” 说明她难以表达自己的想法，所以选B。A、C、D在文中均无依据。

questions.question: What does the star symbolize for Lily?
choices: A. A distant dream she can never reach.
B. A friend who gives her advice.
C. A source of courage and inspiration.
D. A reminder of her fear of speaking.
questions.explanation: 推断题。文中多次提到莉莉从星星那里获得力量，如“she began to believe that she could shine too”和结尾“It had been waiting for her to find her own voice”。星星象征勇气和灵感，故选C。A、B、D与文意不符。

questions.question: What can we infer about Lily's classmates from the story?
choices: A. They were not interested in stars at all.
B. They had never expected Lily to speak so well.
C. They often made fun of Lily's shyness.
D. They knew Lily loved stars before her speech.
questions.explanation: 推断题。第五段说“Her classmates listened in surprise. They had never heard Lily say so much.” 说明同学们对莉莉的出色表现感到意外，因此可以推断他们没想到莉莉能讲得这么好，选B。A、C、D在文中没有明确依据。

title: S — The Silent Squirrel
text:
In the heart of the ancient forest, a squirrel named Silas lived in the hollow of a towering oak. Unlike his chatterbox kin, Silas was mute—not by choice, but by a quirk of nature. While others chirped and scolded, he communicated through subtle movements: a flick of his bushy tail, a tilt of his head, a gentle paw on a friend's shoulder. The other squirrels, accustomed to noisy banter, often overlooked him, assuming his silence meant emptiness.

One autumn, as the leaves turned crimson and gold, a strange blight struck the forest. Acorns, the squirrels' main source of winter food, became scarce. Panic spread through the community. The elders called a meeting, but their frantic screeches only sowed more confusion. Silas watched from a branch, his dark eyes absorbing every detail. He had noticed something the others had missed: the blight was not uniform. Near the stream, where the soil was damp, the acorns remained plump and healthy.

Silas decided to act. He scurried to the stream, gathered a mouthful of good acorns, and returned to the clearing. There, he dropped them at the feet of the elders. The squirrels fell silent, staring at the offering. Then, without a word, Silas turned and bounded back toward the stream, his tail waving like a banner. Curious, a few followed. They found him digging a small cache, carefully storing the precious nuts. Understanding dawned: the stream's moisture had protected the trees.

But the blight was spreading. The healthy grove was small, and the community was large. A debate erupted: should they guard the grove selfishly, or share it? The elders argued, their voices rising. Silas, unable to speak, felt a pang of frustration. Then he had an idea. He gathered the squirrels and led them to a patch of bare earth. With his paws, he drew a map: the stream, the grove, and the surrounding barren land. He pointed to the grove, then to each squirrel, and finally to a spot where they could plant acorns in the spring. His message was clear: the grove was not just for now, but for the future.

Inspired, the squirrels organized. They rationed the acorns, leaving some to plant. They took turns guarding the grove from birds and other animals. Silas, though silent, became the strategist, using his observations to guide their efforts. Winter came, harsh but manageable. The community survived.

Spring arrived, and the squirrels planted the remaining acorns along the stream. Years passed, and a new grove grew, lush and resilient. The forest thrived once more. The squirrels never forgot Silas's lesson: sometimes, the quietest voice speaks the loudest. And Silas, the mute squirrel, had taught them that wisdom is not in noise, but in noticing.
translation:
在古老森林的中心，一只名叫赛拉斯的松鼠住在一棵高耸的橡树的树洞里。与那些叽叽喳喳的同类不同，赛拉斯是沉默的——不是出于选择，而是天性的一个怪癖。当其他松鼠啁啾、斥责时，他通过微妙的动作交流：蓬松尾巴的一甩，头的一歪，爪子轻轻搭在朋友的肩上。其他松鼠习惯了吵闹的玩笑，常常忽略他，以为他的沉默意味着空洞。

一个秋天，当树叶变成深红色和金色时，一场奇怪的枯萎病袭击了森林。橡子，松鼠的主要冬季食物，变得稀少。恐慌在社区中蔓延。长老们召开会议，但他们疯狂的尖叫声只带来了更多混乱。赛拉斯从树枝上看着，他乌黑的眼睛吸收着每一个细节。他注意到了其他人忽略的事情：枯萎病并不均匀。在小溪附近，土壤潮湿的地方，橡子仍然饱满健康。

赛拉斯决定行动。他匆匆跑到小溪边，收集了一口好橡子，然后回到空地。在那里，他把它们放在长老们的脚下。松鼠们安静下来，盯着这份馈赠。然后，一言不发，赛拉斯转身跳回小溪，他的尾巴像旗帜一样挥舞。出于好奇，一些松鼠跟了上去。他们发现他在挖一个小储藏室，小心地储存着珍贵的坚果。大家明白了：小溪的湿气保护了树木。

但枯萎病在蔓延。健康的树丛很小，而社区很大。一场辩论爆发了：他们应该自私地守护树丛，还是分享？长老们争论着，声音越来越高。赛拉斯，无法说话，感到一阵挫败。然后他有了一个主意。他召集松鼠们，带他们到一片光秃的土地上。他用爪子画了一张地图：小溪、树丛和周围贫瘠的土地。他指向树丛，然后指向每只松鼠，最后指向一个他们可以在春天种植橡子的地方。他的信息很明确：树丛不仅是为了现在，而是为了未来。

受到启发，松鼠们组织起来。他们配给橡子，留下一些用于种植。他们轮流守护树丛，防止鸟类和其他动物。赛拉斯，虽然沉默，却成了战略家，用他的观察指导他们的努力。冬天来了，严酷但尚可应付。社区幸存下来。

春天来了，松鼠们沿着小溪种下了剩余的橡子。几年过去了，一片新的树丛长成了，茂盛而有韧性。森林再次繁荣起来。松鼠们从未忘记赛拉斯的教训：有时，最安静的声音说得最响亮。而赛拉斯，那只沉默的松鼠，教会了他们智慧不在于噪音，而在于观察。

questions.question: Why was Silas considered different from other squirrels?
choices: A. He was mute and communicated through movements.
B. He was the oldest squirrel in the forest.
C. He had a unique fur color.
D. He lived alone in a cave.
questions.explanation: 根据第一段，赛拉斯是沉默的，通过动作交流，与其他叽叽喳喳的松鼠不同。

questions.question: What did Silas notice that others had missed about the blight?
choices: A. The blight affected only oak trees.
B. The blight was caused by insects.
C. The blight was not uniform; near the stream, acorns were healthy.
D. The blight would disappear in winter.
questions.explanation: 第二段提到赛拉斯注意到枯萎病并不均匀，在小溪附近，橡子仍然饱满健康。

questions.question: What is the main lesson the squirrels learned from Silas?
choices: A. Silence is always better than noise.
B. Wisdom comes from noticing, not from making noise.
C. It is important to store food for winter.
D. Only elders can make good decisions.
questions.explanation: 故事结尾点明：智慧不在于噪音，而在于观察。赛拉斯虽然沉默，却通过观察和行动教会了大家这一点。

title: The Tea Party
text:
Lily and her mom went to a tea party in the park last Sunday. The sun was warm. Many people came. They brought tea, cakes, and fruit.

Lily saw a small table under a big tree. An old woman sat there. She had a red teapot and some small cups. "Would you like some tea?" the old woman asked. Lily said yes. The tea was green and smelled like flowers.

"This tea is from my garden," the old woman said. "I grow tea plants at home." Lily was surprised. She thought tea only came from shops.

The old woman gave Lily a small bag of tea. "Take it home. You can make tea for your family." Lily thanked her.

At home, Lily made tea for her mom and dad. She put the tea in hot water. The tea turned green. The room smelled like flowers. Mom and Dad drank the tea. "This is the best tea!" Dad said.

Lily smiled. She learned that good things can come from small gardens, and that a simple gift can make people happy.
translation:
上周日，莉莉和妈妈去公园参加了一个茶话会。阳光温暖。很多人来了。他们带来了茶、蛋糕和水果。

莉莉看见一棵大树下有一张小桌子。一位老妇人坐在那里。她有一个红色的茶壶和几个小杯子。“你想喝点茶吗？”老妇人问。莉莉说好。茶是绿色的，闻起来像花。

“这茶来自我的花园，”老妇人说。“我在家种茶树。”莉莉很惊讶。她以为茶只来自商店。

老妇人给了莉莉一小袋茶。“带回家吧。你可以为你的家人泡茶。”莉莉感谢了她。

在家，莉莉为妈妈和爸爸泡了茶。她把茶放进热水里。茶变成了绿色。房间闻起来像花。妈妈和爸爸喝了茶。“这是最好的茶！”爸爸说。

莉莉笑了。她学到了好东西可以来自小花园，而且一个简单的礼物可以让人们快乐。

questions.question: Where did Lily go last Sunday?
choices: A. To a shop
B. To a park
C. To a school
D. To a garden
questions.explanation: 文章第一句提到 'Lily and her mom went to a tea party in the park last Sunday.'，所以答案是公园。

questions.question: What did the old woman give Lily?
choices: A. A red teapot
B. Some cakes
C. A small bag of tea
D. Some flowers
questions.explanation: 文中提到 'The old woman gave Lily a small bag of tea.'，所以答案是C。

questions.question: What did Lily learn from the tea party?
choices: A. Tea is expensive.
B. Old women are kind.
C. Good things can come from small gardens.
D. Tea only comes from shops.
questions.explanation: 文章最后一句 'She learned that good things can come from small gardens, and that a simple gift can make people happy.' 点明了道理，因此选C。

title: The Telescope
text:
Emma had always been fascinated by the stars. Every clear night, she would stand on her balcony, gazing up at the countless lights scattered across the dark sky. She dreamed of discovering something new, something no one had ever seen before. But without a telescope, her dreams seemed as distant as the stars themselves.

One afternoon, while exploring the attic of her late grandfather's house, Emma found an old wooden box covered in dust. Inside, wrapped in a soft cloth, lay a brass telescope. It was beautifully made, with delicate engravings along its tube. Emma's heart raced. She carefully carried it downstairs and set it up on the balcony. That night, she pointed it at the moon and was amazed by the craters she could see. For weeks, she spent every clear evening observing the sky, learning the names of constellations and tracking the movements of planets.

Then, one chilly October night, as she was scanning a patch of sky near the constellation Pegasus, she noticed a faint, fuzzy spot that didn't seem to belong to any star map she had studied. At first, she thought it was just a smudge on the lens. She cleaned it carefully, but the spot remained. Curious, she noted its position and decided to observe it again the next night. To her surprise, it had moved slightly. Over the following weeks, she tracked its slow journey across the sky.

Emma wrote to a local astronomy club, describing what she had seen. A few days later, she received a reply from Dr. Chen, a retired astronomer. He asked if he could visit and see for himself. When he looked through the telescope, he gasped. 'This is a comet,' he said, 'and it appears to be new. You've made a real discovery!' Emma was thrilled. Dr. Chen explained that new comets were often named after their discoverers. So, at the age of fifteen, Emma became the youngest person ever to have a comet named after her: Comet Emma.

The old telescope had opened a door to the universe for her. But more importantly, it had taught her that curiosity and patience can lead to extraordinary things. And she knew that her journey among the stars had only just begun.
translation:
艾玛一直对星星着迷。每个晴朗的夜晚，她都会站在阳台上，凝视着黑暗天空中散落的无数光点。她梦想着发现一些新的东西，一些从未有人见过的东西。但没有望远镜，她的梦想就像星星本身一样遥远。

一天下午，在探索已故祖父的房子的阁楼时，艾玛发现了一个布满灰尘的旧木箱。里面，用柔软的布包裹着，躺着一台黄铜望远镜。它制作精美，镜筒上刻着精致的图案。艾玛的心跳加速。她小心翼翼地把它搬到楼下，架在阳台上。那天晚上，她把它对准月亮，惊讶地看到了月坑。几周以来，她每个晴朗的夜晚都在观察天空，学习星座的名称，追踪行星的运动。

然后，在一个寒冷的十月夜晚，当她扫描飞马座附近的一片天空时，她注意到一个微弱的、模糊的斑点，似乎不属于她研究过的任何星图。起初，她以为只是镜头上的污迹。她仔细清洁，但斑点仍然存在。出于好奇，她记下了它的位置，决定第二天晚上再观察。令她惊讶的是，它稍微移动了。在接下来的几周里，她追踪着它缓慢穿越天空的旅程。

艾玛写信给当地的天文俱乐部，描述了她所看到的一切。几天后，她收到了退休天文学家陈博士的回复。他问是否可以来访亲眼看看。当他通过望远镜观察时，他倒吸一口气。“这是一颗彗星，”他说，“而且似乎是新的。你有了一个真正的发现！”艾玛激动不已。陈博士解释说，新彗星通常以发现者的名字命名。于是，在十五岁时，艾玛成为有史以来最年轻的以自己名字命名彗星的人：艾玛彗星。

那台旧望远镜为她打开了一扇通往宇宙的大门。但更重要的是，它教会了她，好奇心和耐心可以带来非凡的事物。她知道，她在星辰间的旅程才刚刚开始。

questions.question: What did Emma find in the attic?
choices: A. A book about stars
B. A brass telescope
C. A map of constellations
D. A letter from Dr. Chen
questions.explanation: 细节题。文章第二段提到，艾玛在阁楼里发现了一个旧木箱，里面有一台黄铜望远镜（a brass telescope）。

questions.question: Why did Emma write to the astronomy club?
choices: A. To ask for a new telescope
B. To report a strange object she had seen
C. To join the club
D. To learn about constellations
questions.explanation: 推断题。第三段提到艾玛注意到一个模糊的斑点，并追踪了它的移动；第四段开头说她写信给天文俱乐部描述所见，因此目的是报告她看到的奇怪物体。

questions.question: What is the main lesson of the story?
choices: A. Telescopes are expensive.
B. Old things are valuable.
C. Curiosity and patience can lead to great discoveries.
D. Comets are named after famous people.
questions.explanation: 主旨题。文章最后一段点明主题：好奇心和耐心可以带来非凡的事物（curiosity and patience can lead to extraordinary things）。

title: The Tea That Never Grew Cold
text:
The tea party was not what one would call conventional. For one thing, it was held at four in the morning. For another, the host was a retired railway engineer named Mr. Ashford, who had spent forty years on the Trans-Siberian route and now lived alone in a narrow house beside a forgotten station.

"You're wondering why I've asked you here at this absurd hour," he said, pouring steaming amber liquid into a cracked porcelain cup. "The truth is, I've been waiting for someone to share it with for decades."

His guest, a young journalist named Clara, had come to interview him for a magazine article on eccentric retirees. She had expected a dusty apartment and a vague old man. Instead, she found a man whose eyes sparkled with a strange, almost fierce clarity.

"It's just tea," she said, tentatively lifting the cup.

"Ah, but it isn't," Ashford replied. "This tea has never grown cold, not once in thirty years. I brewed it the night my wife died, and it has remained exactly this temperature ever since."

Clara almost laughed, but the man's face was utterly serious. She took a sip. It was warm—pleasantly, impossibly warm, as if freshly poured. She set the cup down and stared at him.

"You don't believe me," he said, without a hint of offense. "People never do. But consider this: the universe is full of mysteries, and we are merely tourists passing through. Who's to say a pot of tea cannot defy the laws of thermodynamics?"

"Or," Clara said slowly, "who's to say you haven't simply reheated it every morning, and made a story out of grief?"

For a long moment, Ashford said nothing. Then he smiled—a sad, knowing smile. "You're perceptive. I like that. Yes, I reheated it. Every single morning. For thirty years. And every time I did, I remembered her—the way she laughed, the way she'd insist on brewing tea at the most inconvenient hours. The ritual kept her alive in my mind."

He lifted his own cup. "The tea grows cold, Miss Clara. Everything does. But the memory—the memory is the flame that keeps it warm."

Clara wrote her article. It was published in a modest magazine and drew little attention. But she never forgot that morning—the strange house, the impossible tea, the old man who had turned mourning into a quiet, daily ceremony.

Years later, when her own father passed away, she found herself brewing a cup of tea at an odd hour, just to feel close to him. And she understood, at last, what Mr. Ashford had meant.

The tea grew cold, as tea always does. But she drank it anyway.
translation:
这场茶会并不寻常。首先，它是在凌晨四点举行的。其次，主人是一位退休的铁路工程师，名叫阿什福德先生，他曾四十年奔波于西伯利亚大铁路，如今独自住在一座被遗忘的车站旁一所狭小的房子里。

“你在想我为什么会在这么荒唐的时间请你来，”他一边说，一边将冒着热气、琥珀色的液体倒入一只开裂的瓷杯。“事实上，我已经等了几十年，想找个人一起分享这件事。”

他的客人是一位名叫克拉拉的年轻记者，来为杂志写一篇关于古怪退休老人的文章而采访他。她本以为会见到一个满是灰尘的公寓和一位含糊其辞的老人。没想到，她见到的是一个眼神中闪烁着奇异而近乎灼热的清明之光的男人。

“这只是茶而已，”她试探性地举起杯子说。

“啊，但这可不是，”阿什福德回答。“这茶从未冷过，三十年来一次都没有。这是我妻子去世那晚我泡的，而它从那以后一直保持着这个温度。”

克拉拉差点笑出来，但男人的表情极其严肃。她抿了一口。茶是温热的——令人愉悦、不可思议地温热，仿佛刚刚倒出。她放下杯子，盯着他。

“你不相信我，”他说，没有一丝被冒犯的样子。“人们从来不信。但想想看：宇宙充满了奥秘，我们不过是路过的游客。谁能说一壶茶就不能违抗热力学定律呢？”

“或者，”克拉拉缓缓说道，“谁能说你不是每天早上把它重新加热，然后用悲伤编了个故事呢？”

阿什福德沉默了许久。然后他笑了——一个悲伤而了然的微笑。“你很有洞察力。我喜欢这一点。是的，我重新加热了它。每天早上。三十年来。而每一次，我都想起了她——她笑的样子，她坚持要在最不方便的时间泡茶的样子。这个仪式让她在我的心中活着。”

他举起自己的杯子。“茶会变冷，克拉拉小姐。一切都会。但记忆——记忆是让它保持温暖的火焰。”

克拉拉写了她的文章。它发表在一本不太起眼的杂志上，没有引起多少关注。但她从未忘记那个早晨——那座奇怪的房子，那杯不可能的茶，那个把哀悼变成安静日常仪式的老人。

多年后，当她自己的父亲去世时，她发现自己在奇怪的时间泡了一杯茶，只为感觉离他更近一些。她终于明白了阿什福德先生的意思。

茶终究会冷，正如茶总是如此。但她还是把它喝完了。

questions.question: Why did Mr. Ashford claim the tea never grew cold?
choices: A. Because he had a magical teapot.
B. Because he reheated it every morning as a ritual to remember his wife.
C. Because the tea was made from a special herb.
D. Because he wanted to impress Clara with a supernatural story.
questions.explanation: 细节题。文中阿什福德承认他每天早上都重新加热茶，以此纪念妻子。A、C、D 均与原文不符。

questions.question: What does Clara initially suspect about Mr. Ashford's story?
choices: A. That he is lying to protect his privacy.
B. That he is suffering from dementia.
C. That he has reheated the tea and created a story out of grief.
D. That he is trying to sell her a magical teapot.
questions.explanation: 推断题。克拉拉在听故事后说：“谁能说你不是每天早上把它重新加热，然后用悲伤编了个故事呢？”表明她怀疑茶是重新加热的，故事源于悲伤。

questions.question: What is the main theme of the story?
choices: A. The importance of drinking tea at unusual hours.
B. The struggle of journalists to find interesting stories.
C. The power of memory and ritual to keep loved ones alive in our hearts.
D. The scientific impossibility of perpetual warmth.
questions.explanation: 主旨题。故事通过阿什福德先生用每日加热茶的仪式怀念妻子，以及克拉拉后来效仿，表达了记忆和仪式能让逝者在心中永存的主题。

title: Under the Umbrella
text:
It was a rainy Monday morning. Lily walked to school with a small red umbrella. The rain was heavy, and the wind was strong.

On the way, she saw an old man. He stood under a tree, but the rain still fell on him. He had no umbrella. Lily walked to him and said, "Sir, please take my umbrella."

The old man smiled. "Thank you, little girl. But what about you? You will get wet."

Lily thought for a moment. Then she said, "Let's walk together. My school is near. We can share the umbrella."

So they walked together. The old man held the umbrella, and Lily walked close to him. They talked about the rain and the flowers. The old man said he was going to the hospital to see his wife. She was ill.

When they got to the hospital, the old man said, "Thank you, Lily. You are very kind." Lily smiled and ran to school. She was a little wet, but she felt happy.

After school, Lily walked home. The rain stopped, and the sun came out. She saw a small box in front of her door. She opened it. Inside, there was a new blue umbrella and a note. The note said, "For the girl with the warm heart. From the old man and his wife."

Lily smiled. She looked at the red umbrella. It was old, but it made her happy. She put the blue umbrella next to it. "Two umbrellas," she said. "One for me, and one for someone who needs it."

From that day, Lily always looked for people without umbrellas.
translation:
那是一个下雨的星期一早晨。莉莉带着一把小红伞走路去上学。雨很大，风也很猛。

在路上，她看到一位老人。他站在一棵树下，但雨还是落在他身上。他没有伞。莉莉走过去对他说：“先生，请拿我的伞吧。”

老人笑了。“谢谢你，小姑娘。但你怎么办呢？你会淋湿的。”

莉莉想了一会儿。然后她说：“我们一起走吧。我的学校很近。我们可以共用这把伞。”

于是他们一起走。老人撑着伞，莉莉紧挨着他走。他们聊着雨和花。老人说他要去看他的妻子。她生病了。

他们到了医院时，老人说：“谢谢你，莉莉。你非常善良。”莉莉笑了笑，跑向学校。她有点湿，但她感到很开心。

放学后，莉莉走回家。雨停了，太阳出来了。她看到门前有一个小盒子。她打开它。里面有一把新的蓝伞和一张纸条。纸条上写着：“给那位心地温暖的女孩。来自老人和他的妻子。”

莉莉笑了。她看着那把红伞。它很旧，但它让她开心。她把蓝伞放在它旁边。“两把伞，”她说，“一把给我，一把给需要的人。”

从那天起，莉莉总是寻找没有伞的人。

vocabulary.meaning: 大的；沉重的（文中指雨大）

questions.question: What is the story mainly about?
choices: A. A girl who sells umbrellas.
B. A girl who helps an old man in the rain.
C. An old man who goes to school.
D. A rainy day at home.
questions.explanation: 文章主要讲述莉莉在雨中帮助一位老人，并与他共用雨伞的故事。

questions.question: Why did the old man go to the hospital?
choices: A. To see his wife.
B. To see a doctor for himself.
C. To buy an umbrella.
D. To meet Lily.
questions.explanation: 文中老人说“he was going to the hospital to see his wife. She was ill.”，因此选A。

questions.question: What can we learn from the story?
choices: A. Rainy days are always bad.
B. Old people need new umbrellas.
C. Kindness brings happiness.
D. Schools are near hospitals.
questions.explanation: 莉莉帮助老人后感到开心，并收到了感谢的礼物，说明善良会带来快乐。

title: U — The Umbrella That Came Back
text:
Mia had never liked umbrellas. They were awkward, easy to lose, and always turned inside out in the wind. But on the day she left for university, her grandmother pressed a small folding umbrella into her hands. "Take it," Grandma said. "You never know when the sky will change its mind." Mia rolled her eyes but packed it anyway.

University life was busier than she had expected. Between lectures, part-time work, and new friends, she barely had time to call home. The umbrella stayed at the bottom of her bag, forgotten. Then one rainy afternoon, she left it on a bus. She realized it only when she got to her apartment, wet and annoyed. "It was just an umbrella," she told herself, but somehow she felt a small, sharp loss.

Weeks passed. Midterms arrived, and with them a wave of stress. Mia's grades were okay, but she felt lonely in a way she hadn't admitted to anyone. One evening, she sat in a café near campus, staring at her laptop and feeling sorry for herself. An old man at the next table noticed her face and smiled kindly. "Rough day?" he asked. Mia nodded. Without saying much more, he told her a short story about a young man who had once lost something important and then found it years later, in a place he had never expected.

Mia didn't think much about it until she stood up to leave. The old man pointed at her chair. Hanging on the back was a small folding umbrella—bright blue, with a tiny embroidered flower near the handle. Her heart jumped. It was exactly like the one she had lost. She looked at the old man, but he had already turned away, reading his newspaper. On the table, where his cup had been, lay a small card. It read: "Lost things often return when you stop chasing them. Go home this weekend."

Mia stood there for a long moment. Then she took out her phone and called her grandmother. The next Saturday, she took the train home. On the platform, Grandma was waiting with a wide smile. "You found it," she said quietly. Mia frowned. "Found what?" Grandma laughed. "The reason to come back."

From that day on, Mia kept the blue umbrella in her bag—not because she needed it, but because it reminded her that some things, once given with love, never really leave us.
translation:
米娅从来不喜欢雨伞。它们笨拙，容易丢，还总是在风里被吹翻。但就在她去上大学的那天，奶奶把一把小小的折叠伞塞进她手里。“拿着，”奶奶说。“你永远不知道天空什么时候会变卦。”米娅翻了个白眼，但还是把它装进了行李。

大学生活比她预想的要忙。在课程、兼职和新朋友之间，她几乎没时间给家里打电话。那把伞一直待在包底，被遗忘了。然后在一个下雨的下午，她把它落在了一辆公交车上。直到回到公寓，她又湿又恼，才意识到伞丢了。“不过是一把伞，”她告诉自己，但不知怎的，她感到一阵小小的、尖锐的失落。

几周过去了。期中考试来了，随之而来的是一波压力。米娅的成绩还行，但她感到一种从未向任何人承认过的孤独。一天晚上，她坐在校园附近的一家咖啡馆里，盯着笔记本电脑，自怜自艾。邻桌的一位老人注意到了她的表情，善意地笑了笑。“今天不顺？”他问。米娅点了点头。没多说别的，他给她讲了一个小故事：一个年轻人曾经丢了一件重要的东西，多年后却在一个他从未想过的地方找到了它。

米娅没太在意，直到她起身要走。老人指了指她的椅子。椅背上挂着一把小小的折叠伞——亮蓝色，手柄附近绣着一朵小花。她的心猛地一跳。它和她丢的那把一模一样。她看向老人，但他已经转过身去，读着报纸。在他放杯子的桌上，留着一张小卡片。上面写着：“你不再追逐时，丢失的东西常常会回来。这个周末回家吧。”

米娅在那里站了很久。然后她拿出手机，给奶奶打了电话。下一个周六，她坐火车回了家。在站台上，奶奶带着灿烂的笑容等着。“你找到了，”她轻声说。米娅皱起眉头。“找到什么？”奶奶笑了。“回来的理由。”

从那天起，米娅把那把蓝伞一直放在包里——不是因为她需要它，而是因为它提醒她：有些东西，一旦带着爱被给予，就永远不会真正离开我们。

vocabulary.meaning: 笨拙的；不方便的；难处理的（文中指雨伞用起来不顺手）
里朝外；彻底地（文中指雨伞被风吹翻）
几乎不；勉强（文中指几乎没有时间）
承认；坦白（文中指承认自己孤独）
自怜；为自己感到难过（文中指米娅情绪低落）
艰难的；不愉快的（文中指“今天不顺吗？”）
刺绣；在……上绣花（文中指伞上绣有小花）
追逐；追求（文中指不再执着寻找丢失之物）
站台；月台（文中指火车站台）
提醒；使想起（文中指雨伞让米娅想起爱与牵挂）

questions.question: Why did Mia keep the blue umbrella in her bag at the end of the story?
choices: A. Because she was afraid of rain.
B. Because it was a gift from the old man.
C. Because it reminded her of love and home.
D. Because she could not find another umbrella.
questions.explanation: 文章最后一段明确说，米娅把蓝伞放在包里不是因为需要它，而是因为它提醒她“有些东西，一旦带着爱被给予，就永远不会真正离开我们”。因此选 C。

questions.question: What happened to the umbrella Mia lost on the bus?
choices: A. Her grandmother found it and sent it back.
B. It appeared again in a café, exactly like the lost one.
C. The old man bought her a new one.
D. She never saw it again.
questions.explanation: 文中提到，米娅在咖啡馆起身时，发现椅背上挂着一把与丢失的伞一模一样的小折叠伞，亮蓝色并有绣花。因此选 B。虽然可能是同一把，也可能只是相似，但文中强调的是“exactly like the one she had lost”。

questions.question: What is the main message of the story?
choices: A. Umbrellas are not useful in strong wind.
B. University students should call home more often.
C. Old people often give good advice.
D. Things given with love can bring us back to what matters.
questions.explanation: 故事主旨不在雨伞本身，也不只是“多打电话”，而是通过雨伞和奶奶的礼物表达：带着爱给予的东西会提醒我们真正重要的东西，比如家人和归属感。因此选 D。

title: Under the Umbrella Tree
text:
Lena had always been the kind of person who planned for every conceivable outcome. When she enrolled at the university, she chose a double major in economics and data science, drafted a five-year career roadmap, and even mapped out which coffee shops had the strongest Wi-Fi. Yet the one thing she couldn't schedule was a conversation with her mother, who had been diagnosed with a rare illness the winter before.

Every Sunday, Lena took the bus to the hospital. She would sit by her mother's bed, holding her hand, while the older woman drifted in and out of sleep. One afternoon, her mother whispered, "Under the old umbrella tree in the garden, I buried a tin box when you were six. Find it." Lena assumed it was the fever talking, but the words lodged in her mind like a splinter.

The following weekend, she went to the garden. The umbrella tree—a sprawling sycamore with leaves like open hands—stood exactly where she remembered. She dug near its roots and unearthed a rusty tin box. Inside were dozens of handwritten notes, each one a small piece of advice. "Don't let grades define you." "Call your father more often." "Learn to cook at least one meal that isn't instant noodles." The last note read: "I know you'll be too busy to visit me someday. That's okay. Just remember: life is not a project to be optimized. It's a garden to be tended."

Lena sat under the tree, tears streaming down her face. She had spent years optimizing her life—course schedules, internships, even friendships—as if every choice could be calculated for maximum efficiency. But her mother's words exposed the flaw in her logic. Efficiency was a means, not an end. The end was connection, presence, love.

When she returned to the hospital that evening, she didn't bring her laptop. She didn't check her phone. She simply sat beside her mother and listened to her breathing. For the first time in months, she wasn't thinking about the next task. She was exactly where she needed to be.

Her mother passed away three weeks later. Lena didn't cry at the funeral; she had already shed her tears under the tree. But she kept the tin box on her desk, and whenever she felt overwhelmed by deadlines, she would open it and read a random note. "Life is a garden," she would murmur. "Tend it."

Years later, Lena became a professor of behavioral economics. Her students often asked her why she chose such an impractical field. She would smile and tell them about the umbrella tree. "Because," she said, "the most important data points aren't numbers. They're moments."
translation:
莉娜一直是那种为每一种可能出现的结果都做好计划的人。当她进入大学时，她选择了经济学和数据科学的双学位，制定了五年职业规划，甚至绘制了哪些咖啡店有最强Wi-Fi的地图。然而，她唯一无法安排的是与母亲的对话，母亲在前一年冬天被诊断出患有一种罕见的疾病。

每个星期天，莉娜都会乘公交车去医院。她会坐在母亲的床边，握着她的手，而年长的女人则在睡梦中时醒时睡。一天下午，母亲低声说：“在花园里那棵老伞树下，你六岁时我埋了一个铁盒。找到它。”莉娜以为那是发烧时的胡话，但那些话像一根刺一样扎在她的脑海里。

接下来的周末，她去了花园。那棵伞树——一棵枝叶如张开的手掌般舒展的枫树——正好矗立在她记忆中的位置。她在树根附近挖掘，挖出了一个生锈的铁盒。里面是几十张手写的纸条，每张都是一小段建议。“不要让成绩定义你。”“多给你父亲打电话。”“学会做至少一道不是方便面的饭。”最后一张纸条写着：“我知道有一天你会太忙而无法来看我。没关系。只要记住：生活不是一个需要优化的项目。它是一个需要照料的花园。”

莉娜坐在树下，泪水顺着脸颊流下。她花了数年时间优化自己的生活——课程表、实习，甚至友谊——仿佛每一个选择都可以为了最大效率而计算。但母亲的话暴露了她逻辑中的缺陷。效率是手段，不是目的。目的是联系、陪伴、爱。

那天晚上回到医院时，她没有带笔记本电脑。她没有看手机。她只是坐在母亲身边，听着她的呼吸。几个月来第一次，她没有在想下一个任务。她正好在她需要的地方。

三周后，母亲去世了。莉娜在葬礼上没有哭；她已经在树下流尽了眼泪。但她把铁盒放在书桌上，每当她被截止日期压得喘不过气时，她就会打开它，随机读一张纸条。“生活是一个花园，”她会低声说。“照料它。”

多年后，莉娜成为了一名行为经济学教授。她的学生常常问她为什么选择这样一个不实用的领域。她会微笑着告诉他们关于伞树的事。“因为，”她说，“最重要的数据点不是数字。它们是时刻。”

vocabulary.meaning: 可想象的，可想到的；文中指“每一种能想到的结果”
路线图，规划；文中指“五年职业规划”
（使）固定，卡住；文中指“话语牢牢留在她脑海中”
碎片，刺；文中比喻“像刺一样扎在脑海里”
挖出，发掘；文中指“挖出铁盒”
优化，使最有效；文中指“把生活当作可优化的项目”
缺陷，瑕疵；文中指“逻辑中的缺陷”
效率；文中指“效率是手段而非目的”
被压倒的，不知所措的；文中指“被截止日期压得喘不过气”
不切实际的；文中指“学生认为行为经济学不实用”

questions.question: What is the main theme of the story?
choices: A. The importance of choosing a practical career.
B. The conflict between efficiency and human connection.
C. The difficulty of studying economics and data science.
D. The regret of not visiting a sick parent.
questions.explanation: 文章通过莉娜从追求效率到领悟生活真谛的转变，突出了效率与情感联系之间的冲突，故B正确。A与故事主旨相反；C只是背景；D是情节的一部分，但非主旨。

questions.question: Why did Lena keep the tin box on her desk?
choices: A. To remind herself of her mother's advice.
B. To store her important documents.
C. To show it to her students.
D. To remember her childhood.
questions.explanation: 文中提到“她 keep the tin box on her desk, and whenever she felt overwhelmed... read a random note”，说明她保留铁盒是为了提醒自己母亲的建议，故A正确。B、C、D均非主要目的。

questions.question: What can be inferred about Lena's mother from the notes?
choices: A. She was disappointed in Lena's choices.
B. She wanted Lena to become a professor.
C. She valued life experiences over achievements.
D. She expected Lena to visit her every day.
questions.explanation: 母亲在纸条中写道“不要让成绩定义你”“生活是一个需要照料的花园”，表明她更看重生活体验而非成就，故C正确。A、B、D在文中没有依据。

title: V — The Village Violin
text:
In a small village, there was a girl named Lisa. She loved music. Every evening, she played her violin near the river. The sound was beautiful. Many people came to listen.

One day, a famous violinist, Mr. Brown, visited the village. He heard Lisa play. "You are very good," he said. "You can be a great musician. Come with me to the city. I can teach you."

Lisa was very happy. But she also felt sad. She loved her village. She did not want to leave her family and friends. She asked her mother for advice. Her mother said, "Follow your heart."

Lisa thought for a long time. She wanted to be a great musician. But she also loved her village. Finally, she had an idea. She said to Mr. Brown, "I want to learn, but I want to stay here. Can you come and teach me here?" Mr. Brown was surprised. He thought about it. Then he smiled. "Yes, I can," he said. "I can come every month and teach you. And you can teach the children here."

Lisa was very happy. She learned from Mr. Brown. She also taught the children in the village. Many years later, Lisa became a famous violinist. She never left her village. People came from far away to hear her play. And she always said, "Music is everywhere. You don't have to leave home to find it."
translation:
在一个小村庄里，有一个叫丽莎的女孩。她热爱音乐。每天晚上，她在河边拉小提琴。声音很美。许多人来听。

有一天，一位著名的小提琴家布朗先生来到了这个村庄。他听到丽莎演奏。“你非常棒，”他说。“你可以成为一名伟大的音乐家。跟我去城市吧，我可以教你。”

丽莎非常高兴。但她也感到难过。她爱她的村庄。她不想离开家人和朋友。她向母亲征求意见。母亲说：“跟随你的心。”

丽莎想了很久。她想成为一名伟大的音乐家。但她也爱她的村庄。最后，她有了一个主意。她对布朗先生说：“我想学习，但我想留在这里。你能来这里教我吗？”布朗先生很惊讶。他想了想。然后他笑了。“是的，我可以，”他说。“我可以每个月来教你。你也可以教这里的孩子。”

丽莎非常高兴。她向布朗先生学习。她也教村里的孩子们。许多年后，丽莎成为了一位著名的小提琴家。她从未离开她的村庄。人们从很远的地方来听她演奏。她总是说：“音乐无处不在。你不必离开家去寻找它。”
